subsubtopic: FINANCE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS-SIXTEENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the sixteenth report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.
The report deals with the proposed multistage sales tax that was set out in the White Paper on tax reform. The committee has done a great deal of work on this tax reform paper, including its visit to New Zealand and its fifteenth report.
At this stage, the committee feels that until the Government has completed its negotiations with the provinces for a national sales tax, it would not be appropriate to continue working on the White Paper. The committee states that the Government must give a very high priority to this negotiation for a national sales tax. The consultations that affect parties and the operational detail of that multistage sales tax is urgent in the commercial affairs of the country.

subsubtopic: RESEARCH INTO PREVENTION AND CURE OF SCHIZOPHRENIA
speechtext:

The petitioners believe that a method of prevention and a cure can be found, but only through larger research efforts.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that research efforts relating to schizophrenia will, in

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO BILL C-72-OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present two petitions from a number of residents of Alberta who are concerned that Bill C-72 will set a dangerous precedent by banning unilingual Anglophones and other cultures.
They call upon Parliament to cancel Bill C-72 so that unilingual people have a chance for a position in government.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO THE EXPULSION OF TURKISH NATIONALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to table a petition in the House, pursuant to Standing Order 106. The petition was signed by a number of Montreal residents who would like the Government and, more specifically, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), to consider with the requisite fairness, understanding and dispatch the lot of 2,000 Turkish men, women and children living under the threat of deportation by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard).

subsubtopic: PROHIBITION REGARDING KNIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition, once again from a number of citizens who are concerned about the increase in incidents of crime associated with knives in all major cities across Canada, including murder, robbery, and sexual assault.
They call upon the federal Government and Parliament to amend the Criminal Code to prohibit the carrying of knives by citizens in public places.
Exemptions from this ban would only include those who use knives as part of their legitimate work or when they are carried for religious purposes.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF RIGHTS OF THE UNBORN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a petition from what must be just about every living soul in the communities of Elgin and Mapleton in my constituency of Fundy-Royal.
They implore the House to restore dignity and honour to the country by bringing forth legislation very quickly so that the rights of the unborn can be protected.

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present petitions relative to the Government's signing of a trade deal with the United States.
The petitioners feel that the trade agreement negates the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty, that it would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future, that it would undermine Canada's ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States, and that it would threaten hundreds of thousands of Canadian jobs.
Therefore, the petitioners pray that Parliament dissolve and that the people of Canada have the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

I think it will be debatable and that we can look forward to a very exciting debate today.

Canadian consumers have a tradition of being fair-minded individuals who, on numerous occasions, have been prepared to make sacrifices in view of the public interest. However, they have demonstrated that they do not like unfairness. They do not appreciate unfairness, and they certainly do not appreciate when a national Government purposely sets out to be unfair to them and to their interests.
We have seen that, as a result of the high cost of prescription drugs. We have seen the inadequacies of the postal services. By the end of 1988, between 350,000 and 400,000 Canadians will be without door-to-door mail delivery, having to make do with the so-called supermailboxes. According to current new housing projections, by 1990 the figure will rise to well over 500,000. Also there is the high cost of gasoline, which has risen roughly 23 cents per gallon since the present administration assumed office in 1984.
We also see an unprecedented proliferation of personal taxes on individuals across the board, so much so that they are in excess of some $22 billion.
Of course we have seen the increase in inspector fees in the agricultural sector as it affects people in Prince Edward Island, particularly those in the potato industry. The past four years have been particularly tough for P.E.I. potato farmers. Markets and prices have been better this year, but they are still recovering from their earlier problems.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) was especially insensitive when he decided to increase inspection fees on P.E.I. potatoes bound for other provinces and beyond. In fact, inspection fees have risen from 3 cents per hundredweight in 1987 to 6 cents this year, and by 1990 the fee will be 15 cents per hundredweight.
Supply
We have also seen the imposition of user fees for Atlantic fishermen. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has started to charge even higher fees in some instances for the use of wharf space and facilities. For inshore fishermen who have not caught much fish, these additional charges become what is best known as an enormous burden.
The Government's apparent acquiescence to sky-rocketing bank charges is another example of unfairness being delivered to the Canadian consumer. The Government has failed to take appropriate action with regard to the collapse of the Principal Group. The 67,000 Canadians who invested in these particular companies have not received any assistance from the Government of Canada. Of course, the unnecessary high interest rate policy of the Government of Canada at the present time affects many Canadians and many consumers across the board.
I have outlined a number of major concerns for Canadian consumers, many of which will be touched upon today by myself and by other Members of the House. I would hope that we would give some consideration in a very sincere way to the plight of Canadian consumers, particularly those who were given assurances some time ago by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), and I say this with great sincerity, who has now acquired the name given to him by most individuals of the Minister responsible for the corporate sector. He is no longer the champion of the cause of Canadian consumers. What better evidence do we have than the plight of Canadian consumers and their outrage at the increased cost of prescription drugs?
It was said on numerous occasions in this House when the Bill was being debated in committees of the House as well as of the Upper Chamber, that with the passage of this Bill would come the additional high cost of prescription drugs. The Minister, in his wisdom, on September 6, 1986, -this is the Minister responsible for Canadian consumers-said:
There is absolutely nothing in this Bill that will cause drug prices to go up by a penny.
That was the Minister speaking on September 6, 1986. But the evidence is quite the contrary. The Globe and Mail had something to say. I will quote from the article so that Members will have an opportunity to refer to it later in the debate: It reads:
The prices of more than a thousand pharmaceutical drugs have risen faster than the Consumer Price Index in the past six months. Many of these are brand-name drugs whose manufacturers have given assurances that increases will not exceed the CPI.
Lawrence Archer, a spokesman for the Ontario Health Ministry, said yesterday that 1,099 drugs are more than 5 per cent costlier on this month's price list than they were last July, while the CPI rose by 4.4 per cent. This number makes up almost half the total provincial formulary.
In a few cases drug prices rose by 100 per cent and in one case the increase was 250 per cent, Mr. Archer said. He would not release the name of the drugs in question ...
The Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada which represents the large multinational drug companies, pledged that drug price increases

March 24, 1988

would not outstrip increases in the CPI when it lobbied successfully last fall for
increased patent protection for brand name drugs...
Let us look not only at what the Ontario Ministry of Health has said about the high cost of prescription drugs since the passage of Bill C-22, but let us look at a study of five companies which belong to the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association. I should say at the outset that of the five, Merck Frosst, one company in Canada, which seems rather convincing from my perspective, had reduced the cost of its prescription drugs. This was a study done in the period from January, 1987 to January, 1988. Its prices are based on the manufacturers' published price list. Out of the five, I say to the Minister opposite, one company reduced its prices. The others, however, have had substantial increases. Smith/Kline Company produces Dyazide tablets and the price has gone from $ 14.23 to $15.65, a 9.9 per cent increase. The cost for 100 tablets of Dyrenium has increased 16.6 per cent. For two milligram tablets of Stelazine there is a 17.5 per cent increase. For 200 mg. tablets of Tagamet the cost is up by 10.02 per cent. Those are Smith/Kline products.
Then we come to Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals (Canada) Inc. Again, from January, 1987 to January, 1988, for 500 milligrams of Alertonic, the price has risen from $14.25 to $17.25, an increase of not 2 per cent, not 3 per cent but 21 per cent to the Canadian consumer. Then for 100 tablets of Bentylol Dospan the price has gone up from $19.55 to $25.20, an increase of 28.9 per cent. So much for the commitment of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. So much for the words in September, 1986 that drug prices would not increase in Canada. With the same company in the same time frame, for 50 Clomid tablets the price has risen from $165 to $211.15, an increase of 27.97 per cent. For 12 mg. Tace capsules, the price has gone up from $24.40 to $36.60 for a mere increase of 50 per cent. That is utterly shameful.
Another company which had its drug prices reviewed was Janssen Pharmaceutical Inc., in the same time frame as the other companies. We have a drug here called Innovar and its price has risen from $119.10 to $145.40 for an increase of 22.08 per cent.
What about Sandoz Canada Inc.? For eight tablets of Ancasal the cost was $4.70 cents. It is now up to $6.38 for an increase-this is the fairness for Canadian consumers who were not going to pay one more cent as a result of the passage of Bill C-22-of 35.7 per cent.
I think that is clear and unequivocal evidence that Canadian consumers have been given a snow job by the Canadian Government. The Canadian Government, being apprised of these facts, is sitting back and doing absolutely nothing.
The Nova Scotia Association of Health Organizations says that from March, 1984 to February, 1985 prescription drugs which it handled have increased by 17.5 per cent. From March, 1985 to February, 1986 there is a 13.6 per cent increase. It is just not evidence that the Opposition is taking into the House of Commons. This is information prepared by
Canadians who are directly involved in that particular sector of our economy. I find it to be rather appalling that the Minister has chosen to do absolutely nothing.
In the Upper House, a Bill has been introduced in order to try to give some teeth to what is known as an imperfect, if you will, but at best, a prices review board. The Minister wrongly blames the Opposition for delaying the passage of Bill C-22 and thereby the establishment of the Drug Prices Review Board provided for in the legislation, he says, to control drug prices. Bill C-22 increased patent protection which was given to brand name manufacturers retroactively to June 27, 1986. You would think that that retroactivity would apply to the Drug Prices Review Board which would or may review the price of a drug. The answer is that it does not apply to the Drug Prices Review Board.
My colleagues in the Upper Chamber are attempting to make amendments that would perfect a piece of legislation which has a very strong effect on Canadian consumers. There we have the unfairness which was predicted by opposition Parties, by the United Church, by the Royal Canadian Legion, by consumer groups and by senior citizens across Canada.
The collapse of the Principal Group of companies and the
67,000	investors who have lost in many instances their life savings is but another example of the Canadian Government's refusing to accept responsibility or refusing to become involved in what is none other than a national disgrace. I do not have to remind you, Sir, as a very able representative from the Province of Alberta, how these investors feel at this time. However, the response of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has been: "Well, it's not my problem. I didn't do it, the devil did it. Don't come to me, I'm not responsible. I don't want to be involved. That is a provincial matter".
I say to the Minister that that is a cop-out. The Minister knows that only too well. In his hands, he has a report from the CDIC, but he says, and I applaud him for this, that he cannot publish the report of the CDIC because that would breach confidentiality and, as a Minister of the Crown, he could not do that. I understand that argument. I do, and I have said that to the Minister. He does not wish to acknowledge that, but I have.
I have also said to the Minister that the interest of the public carries more weight than the confidentiality of a particular company or companies, because there are 67,000 Canadians who have lost their life savings. The paramount action the Minister ought to take is to make that report public so that Canadians may see what information the CDIC had and what it did with that information. That would send a signal to the financial community that the Government of Canada will not tolerate those companies, which may be in a minority but which cause Canadians to question both the ethics and the integrity of many financial institutions.
March 24, 1988

The Minister will rise and do a step-dance, the twist, the limbo and all sorts of dances to try to put it on the Alberta Government. He will try to put it on the need for new federal regulations, etc., etc., but the fact is that the Minister and the Government had an opportunity, and still have an opportunity, to help Canadian consumers who were affected by the collapse of the Principal Group.
As recently as yesterday, we heard of the taxes that Revenue Canada is forcing these Canadian consumers to pay. I am happy to read in the paper that the Minister will be making a decision on that within a very short period of time.
The litany of things that the Government has done to Canadian consumers goes on and on. I know that there are some in this House who are intimately concerned and have voiced their concerns over bank charges. I do not want to say anything about the snarky letter I received from the Royal Bank of Canada on March 22, 1988. I do not want to talk about the contents of that letter in which the author admits that there are bank charges and that there is a charge of $85 for the signing of mortgage renewal documents. The Government seems, by its conduct and its lack of action, to acquiesce to sky-rocketing bank charges.
If the Minister does not think that this is such a serious issue, let me tell him about a letter from the Royal Bank of Canada dated December 14, 1987, addressed to an individual and signed by a manager of the Royal Bank of Canada. The manager says in the letter that effective November 1, 1987, the bank began levying a charge for providing information via the telephone to its clients. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what the Royal Bank, as of January 1, 1988, is charging Canadians for information on their accounts that they may seek by telephone? It is charging $5 a pop.
Of course, the Minister sits back in his Gucci office, wonderful surroundings, and says: "Oh, well, let the consumers have it". There is the fairness that Canadian consumers are getting from the Government.
What about the tax increases that have affected Canadian consumers from coast to coast? There has been an unprecedented number of new taxes imposed on Canadian consumers.
I	think it is worth mentioning, for the benefit of Hon. Members, that sales taxes went from 9 per cent to 10 per cent on October 1, 1984. They were upped again from 10 per cent to
II	per cent on January 1, 1986. Again they were upped on April 1, 1986, from 11 per cent to 12 per cent. Sales taxes have gone up from 9 per cent to 12 per cent.
What has this great Government which has so much concern for Canadian consumers, done? It has extended the sales tax to candy, soft drinks, fast foods and snacks. It has increased from 8 per cent to 12 per cent the tax on paint and wallpaper, and the Tory tax has even taken a new twist. The Tories have now gone after toys for kids.

The Minister laughs. I know that you are not laughing, Mr. Speaker, because you know that the unfairness of these measures will be brought to bear in the next federal election.
I have already mentioned the increases in gasoline taxes, that of 23 cents per gallon over the last four years. The taxes go on and on. I know that there are many more Hon. Members in the House who will want to participate in this debate, so I will sum up.
It has been clear, since September of 1984, that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has devoted his time and his energy to promoting and enhancing the corporate interests of Canada to the detriment of Canadian consumers. We have seen it with prescription drugs, with bank charges, with inspectors' fees, with wharfage fees for Atlantic fishermen, with unprecedented tax increases, and with the lack of concern for the 67,000 investors affected by the collapse of the Principal Group of companies. That is a summary of my argument, and I would hope that the Government would assume its responsibilities for consumers as it has assumed its responsibilities for protecting and enhancing corporate interests. It is high time the consumers got a fair shake.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to ask the Hon. Member a question about the apples and oranges comparison he was making on drug prices at the beginning of his speech. The 1987 prices were compared to the 1988 prices. Would the Hon. Member tell me if he was comparing the manufacturers' level of 1987 with the retail level of 1988? If he was, he was misleading the House by saying that there has been an increase, because the increases would be calculated on a different basis.
Second, would the Hon. Member confirm that the report he is quoting containing these misleading indicators was commissioned by Senator Haidasz, a Liberal Member of the Senate? Could he confirm too that the 1987 prices he quoted contained no federal sales taxes but that he quoted a 1988 price which included sales tax?
Finally, a number of the drugs he mentioned are now off patent, and the generic companies could copy them if they wanted to. That point, of course, was made by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) a few days ago. Can he confirm that he heard that from the Minister?

Mr. Speaker, there were several questions there. To alleviate the fear and ooziness in the Minister's mind, I would be happy to show him a copy of the report I referred to. The report deals with pricing from January, 1987, to January, 1988. The prices are based on the manufacturers' published price list. Yes, the report was prepared with respect to the impact of the proclamation of Bill C-22 on drug prices. It was prepared for Senator Stanley Haidasz by two pharmacists. As soon as I give it to the Hansard people the Minister will have an opportunity to read it at his leisure.

March 24, 1988

With respect to the high cost of prescription drugs, I want to remind the Minister that we said very clearly in committee and in this House that drug prices would increase, not only brand-name drugs but generic drugs. The reason is, and the Minister ought to focus on this, that the brand-name companies would have a period of exclusivity for upwards of 10 years. The only way the generic companies could maintain their viability in the short term was either to lay off people or to increase their prices. We do not agree with it but that is what is happening. It is happening not only to generic drugs but to brand-name drugs as well. We told the Government, and witnesses told the Government, that that is what would happen if it tried to move from the old system to one involving exclusivity for the brand-name companies.
The Minister also referred to certain comments that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs made in the House. Yes, I am well aware of those comments. I am also well aware of the undertakings that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs gave to the committee, to Parliament, the committee in the other place, and Canadians generally that prescription drug prices would not increase one red cent. That was his September 6, 1986 statement.

Mr. Speaker, I would draw to your attention and that of the Hon. Member that the motion speaks to the abject failure of the Government to protect the best interests of Canadian consumers because of its unnecessarily high interest rate policy, among other things. Over the last few weeks I have been pressing the Government to bring interest rates down from the current bank rate of 8.5 per cent or so and mortgage rates of 10.5 per cent to 11.5 per cent. I believe they are unnecessarily high. However, I have a recollection that under the Liberal Government, of which the Hon. Member was a supporter, interest rates went up to 20 per cent and to 22 per cent, and mortgage rates hit 19 per cent or 20 per cent.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member if he agrees that interest rates are unnecessarily high at just over 8 per cent for T-bills and 10.5 per cent to 11.5 per cent for mortgages. If so, why did he not speak out in the early 1980s at the time his Government arbitrarily imposed a tight money policy and applied monetarism with the utmost rigour to the point at which farmers, small businesses and consumers were forced to the wall? People across the country lost their homes because they could not afford the high interest rates. Where was the Hon. Member then and why was he not speaking out in order to bring those interest rates down?
Mr. Speaker, it is always nice to be able to respond to a question from the NDP.
Be nice, Dave.
They are the ones who-
Ask Howard Pawley.
Precisely. I guess you could ask Howard Pawley a number of questions.
Give us your answer.

I will respond to the Hon. Member. There is no question that interest rates now as well as at the time he referred to are and were unnecessarily high. The Hon. Member may have been here, and if he was not, he may not be aware of the fact that at that time we had a world-wide recession.
Oh, oh!

Hon. Members may wish to try and poke holes in that, but the fact remains. We saw it in the energy sector and we saw it in interest rate policies not only in Canada but in the U.S. The Government is now preaching that we are in a position of economic strength. Yet we see the spreading to Canada of the unnecessarily high interest rate policy in the U.S.
The Hon. Member may be trying to take credit for things he may or may not have brought up on the floor of the House of Commons. I do not recall if he did, although I accept his word. Hopefully he will accept my word that my colleague from Laval-des-Rapides also raised that point on the floor of the House of Commons. The Hon. Member ought not to-
Not when the Liberals were in power.
He was not a Member then. The Hon. Member ought not to speak with a forked tongue.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member on his brilliant and most remarkable speech, especially the part about drugs, since as he said so aptly, at the time the legislation was considered in the House, everyone expected some very substantial increases. He made it clear that not only did this happen, but it happened faster, and more ruthlessly.
I have another example. I received a telephone call this morning in my riding office, about a woman who is planning to adopt a young Mexican boy. Immigration Canada says it will charge her $185 to open a file. There is a whole series of similar charges which, added to the ruthless measures I mentioned earlier, will put an incredibly heavy tax burden on consumers generally.
The Government's reaction seems to be: Don't worry. We are going to solve all our problems with free trade which will provide the framework for substantial improvements at the consumer level.
The question I would like to ask my colleague is: Does he feel that free trade will eventually bring about improvements for the Canadian consumer?
March 24, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raised a number of important issues. In many instances the cost of prescription drugs is borne by provincial Governments. That is why, if you check the record, you will find that numerous provinces, although not all, have objected to the thrust of Bill C-22. Clearly, in their mind and in the minds of others the Bill caused an unnecessarily large increase in the cost of drugs. They will have to deal with that either through new taxes or through cutting back on health services.
I have often, in committee and in this House, given Nova Scotia as an example of the problem. That small province may have to pay upwards of $25 million in excess costs because of Bill C-22. The province will have to go after the taxpayers in some form to recoup that money.
With regard to the free trade agreement and how that will affect Canadian consumers, I think we have seen evidence of that already. If we have to be on a level playing field with our friends to the south, we will have to pay more in some areas. There is, though, a historical argument that free trade and the lessening of tariffs will provide benefits to Canadian consumers.
Yes.
Does that mean, however, that we are going to lose jobs as a result of this? The answer is very clearly yes. Therefore, the effect on the Canadian economy is negative.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to participate in this debate today. This debate is about the interest of Canadian consumers. The resolution is a bit of a mishmash and it is difficult to know what the focus of the Hon. Member's motion is. George Bernard Shaw once apologized to someone to whom he was writing a letter saying that he was sorry that he did not have time to write a brief letter and would, therefore, write a long letter.
This is a lengthy motion which shows a lack of focus and clarity of thought on a question of real importance to Canadians in their role as consumers. He tried to argue that in nine different policy areas there is some unreasonable burden placed on the consumer, and I will address those in my formal remarks.
We do not have in this debate a speech from the Liberal Party which can be taken credibly because of the record of that Party and indeed of the Hon. Member on consumer issues. The voting record of the Hon. Member shows that he has quite consistently overlooked great opportunities to defend the Canadian consumer.
For example, he voted against increased competition in the air and rail transportation sector by voting against Bill C-18 in the second session of this Parliament. He voted against
Supply
increased competition in extra provincial trucking by voting against Bill C-19 in the second session of this Parliament. The Hon. Member had an opportunity to do something about consumers' rights on the pharmaceutical issue. He spent a great deal of time speaking about that today but he did not answer my questions, and I hope you noticed that, Mr. Speaker.
When I made the point that he was comparing apples and oranges, he avoided answering that directly. He is comparing one year with the sales tax with another without sales tax, and one year at the manufacturers' level with another at the retail level. It is misleading to quote statistics which do not have a common base. Perhaps when the Hon. Member has an opportunity to ask me questions he will respond to that question which I put to him and to which he did not respond.
The Member had a chance to vote for a Drug Prices Review Board when we brought in Bill C-22. This federal board will be in place to exercise a downward pressure on all drug prices, not only generically copied drugs. This is a huge venture on behalf of the consumer, but he voted against it.
The Member also had an opportunity to vote for the compensation of the uninsured depositors of two western banks, but he did not do so. He voted against the privatization of Teleglobe Canada. The sale of that Crown corporation has resulted in significantly low rates for overseas telephone calls.
I am suggesting that the Hon. Member is not always as alert to interests of consumers as he likes to assert he is. Indeed, his Party is not, and I can therefore understand why he has some difficulty in being alert to their interests.
His comments today invite deliberate and careful answers from me. However, this does give me occasion to talk about the consumer in a wider context than these picayune little details that he raises in his motion. Quite frankly, the failure of the Opposition to mount a coherent case against the Government's economic policies is evident every day in this House, and this failure could hardly be better illustrated than by the grab-bag of items before the House today. The idea seems to be that what you lack in the quality of criticism you can make up for in quantity.
This just does not work because the Government's economic policies have worked from the day we came into office, are working today, and will continue to work for the good of Canadians in every part of the country. I can say that with every conviction because our policies are working. It is very difficult to find any economic indicator which affects the average Canadian as a consumer which is not immensely better year over year and immensely better than it was five years ago.

Like the unemployment rate in Newfoundland?

March 24, 1988

The unemployment rate in Newfoundland is a good example. It, too, has improved year after year since we have been in government.
It's at an intolerable level, and you know it.

Noting the range of subjects which the motion has grouped together you will not be surprised, Mr. Speaker, that some specific areas will be discussed by other speakers for the Government today.
To begin with, let us be clear about the Canadian consumers referred to in the motion. Contrary to the impression which the Hon. Member tried to leave, they are not some special interest group with particular interests separate from those of everyone else. All Canadians are consumers. More to the point, their present and future well-being as consumers depends directly on the ability of the Canadian economy to produce new jobs and to produce higher incomes and new economic opportunities now and in the years ahead. Consumers are not only people dealt with by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs but are consumers in the wider sense which I just mentioned.
The kind of negative thinking which is reflected in the motion before us today was soundly rejected by Canadians in September, 1984. Instead of approaching government this way they wanted a positive new approach to the economic challenges facing Canada. That is exactly what the Government has provided. We did not do this in an ad hoc way. We made clear to the Canadian people how we were going to proceed. We laid it out clearly in the agenda for economic renewal in
1984.	It is there for everyone to see.
Often governmental statements of that nature under Liberal Governments did not mean anything, they were mere cream puffs with very little substance and certainly not followed through seriously by the Government. In this case the agenda for economic renewal is truly a blueprint. The governmental engineers have gone to work with it and have built an edifice which is very impressive. We have stuck to our program, and the results more than bear out the success of our policies. In every instance the consumer wins.
As an example of how the consumer wins, in 1987 real growth in gross domestic product reached 3.9 per cent, a growth rate higher than that of the United States. That was the third consecutive year in which growth was in that range. That is a tremendous performance.
Interest rates, too, have been stable at three to four percentage points below the levels reached in September, 1984. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) reminded the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) of this. Interest rates are much lower today than they were in September, 1984. Real interest rates are also down substantially in the same period, to the benefit of the Canadian economy as a whole and of Canadians in their role as consumers. Nothing is more difficult for consumers to cope with than high interest rates, and we have brought them down.
The typical five-year mortgage rate is a good example. It is now 11 per cent down from 14.25 per cent in 1984. What could be more relevant to a consumer than that? This represents a saving of $1,400 per year on a $50,000 mortgage amortized over 25 years. Is the Hon. Member against that kind of action on behalf of the consumer? Consumers are also homeowners. Houses needed to be built so that they can have a choice. Housing starts are up from 135,000 in 1984 to 246,000 last year, which is the highest annual level for housing starts since 1977. Nothing could be more important to consumers than that figure.
Of course, consumers must be employed. The unemployment rate is down to 8.9 per cent in 1987 from 11.3 per cent in 1984 when we took over from the Hon. Member's Party as Government. It was down even further, to 7.8 per cent in February of this year. In response to the interjection by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, the unemployment rate is down in all provinces, which is good news for Newfoundlanders as well as people from all other provinces.
The decline in the unemployment rate reflects a tremendous achievement in job creation. February is the seventeenth consecutive month in which full-time employment increased. Since September, 1984, 1.213 million jobs have been created. That is what we have accomplished for Canadian consumers.
The growth in our gross domestic product in recent years has put us in the top rank of leading industrialized nations. In fact, people who study Canada are impressed with what they see. The latest survey of business investment intentions is a good example. While such news may not make the front page, it is astonishing that Canadian business is planning to increase its investment in plant and equipment by an extraordinary 17.3 per cent this year. Usually increased investment intentions are up by 2 per cent or 3 per cent, if at all, over the previous year. This is the largest real increase in private sector investment spending in nine years. We have achieved those results because we took the necessary action to ensure a positive environment for job creating growth and investment.
We have made substantial progress in deficit reduction and controlling the growth of the debt, thereby reducing the burden on the consumer who must ultimately pay the bills.
In anticipation of what might be said by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, I should remind the House what happened under an NDP Government in Manitoba with regard to debts and deficits. The NDP often tells us that we should increase government spending for one reason or another. However, we hear very little about how they would raise the revenue to do it.
Why do you not talk about Saskatchewan first? Then we will talk about Manitoba.

I often hypothesize about what they would do if they were in power.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I trust that on a day like today, when we have had a national prayer breakfast, we would be able to wait until the Hon. Minister has finished debate. We will be able to have questions and comments after the speech. The Hon. Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hoc kin).

Mr. Speaker, these are sensitive matters to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre, but they must be discussed. In Manitoba, spending has increased from 18.5 per cent of GDP to 21.3 per cent, relative to the size of the economy. If the NDP Government in Manitoba had simply held spending growth to the rate of nominal economic growth, the present revenue structure would now yield a $250 million surplus rather than a $334 million deficit.
We hear talk about the NDP Government being the protectors of the consumer. The Crown corporation in that province which provides automobile insurance has acquired a $60 million operating deficit, which has led to premium increases of between 18 per cent and 112 per cent to the consumer in Manitoba. That is what an NDP Government delivers. Government automobile insurance in Winnipeg is now more expensive than private sector insurance in Ottawa. That is a very important fact to keep in mind when the NDP rises to defend the consumer. Last December, the NDP Government wrote off $185 million in Crown corporation losses by Order in Council. This is not shown on the government books as either a government expenditure or as a Crown corporation loss.
Provincial government revenues in Manitoba have increased by 94 per cent over the past seven years, more than twice the 42 per cent increase in consumer prices that have occurred over the same period. While there is supposed to be an NDP Government in power to protect the consumer, there is no protection whatsoever. As a matter of fact, I cannot imagine what would happen if that kind of laboratory experiment were applied by the NDP at the federal level.
We have fostered a healthy and receptive climate by controlling the deficit. We have brought it down for four years in a row by controlling the growth of debt and reducing the burden on consumers who must ultimately pay the bill. It is the consumers of Manitoba who will have to pay the bill for what the NDP Government did there.
We have fostered a healthy and very receptive climate for private sector investment, a fact which the opposition Parties have neglected to acknowledge. We know that the private sector is the engine of growth in the economy, not the Government.
We also reduced the burden of government intervention through deregulation. While that may not interest the Opposition, it is a very important step in order to let fresh air blow through the economy and protect the consumer.
We established a new policy to promote the development of science and technology. We are encouraging innovation. We
Supply
have made regional development more sensitive to local needs. Through a combination of responsible fiscal, monetary and economic policies, the Government has provided a stable framework for economic progress, which has been of tremendous value to Canadians in their roles as consumers.
We have undertaken a major reform of the tax system. This is being done with Canadian consumers in mind. Our tax system will now be better balanced and fair. Previous Liberal Governments never did anything in terms of establishing a comprehensive and coherent way to make the tax system more balanced and fair.
As a result of our action to reduce tax rates and broaden the tax base, 85 per cent of all households, or 9.7 million, will see their tax reduced. Moreover, 850,000 lower-income Canadians will have their taxes reduced to zero.
As a result of our changes our tax system will lose many of its complicated deductions and its elaborate system of tax brackets. Lower personal income tax rates mean that Canadians will keep more of every additional dollar of earnings, which is perhaps the big message in tax reform. People will now be able to keep more of what they earn so that they can go into the world as consumers with more to spend. That is the purpose of tax reform. Tax reform means more money to save or spend as the consumer sees fit.
Tax reform also means that corporations pay more while individuals pay less. This is not mentioned by the Opposition, but it is a very fundamental reform. We can implement a more progressive tax system that is more efficient and can better encourage the productive economic activity on which all Canadians depend for economic well-being.
This first stage of tax reform is designed neither to increase nor to decrease revenues. In the same way, reform of the sales tax system will also be fiscally neutral. This is important if we are to succeed in the highly competitive international market. Obviously, the over-all thrust of tax reform is in the interest of Canadians as consumers.
Let me turn to the financial institution sector about which the Hon. Member raises questions. I know he is interested in the financial institution sector. Because we had a number of Bills passed at the end of the last session, I think it is important for me to remind the Hon. Member of Bill C-42 and Bill C-56. They speak to the concerns he raised today. The Hon. Member was not there to vote on them, and I am sorry he was not because in fact he would see that we have set up a CDIC which can play a much greater role in our financial system.
We have also established a supervisor of financial institutions who will be able to make our system far more efficient and fair to the consumer and to Canadians when they look for credit or want to deposit. Above all-and this is very important for Canadians as consumers-these two Bills will make the system safer so we will not have these Principal Group

kinds of disasters. The Hon. Member knows that the Principal Group is made up of 127 companies, only one of which is federally insured through CDIC. He wants to tar the federal Government with the brush of all 127 companies, and that is irresponsible.

speechtext: I regret but the Hon. Minister's time has expired. I would just like to say that I did give the first speaker additional time and the Minister was also given additional time. I will now recognize Hon. Members on questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister and I can disagree on various points. I disagree emphatically with the concept of the Drug Prices Review Board within Bill C-22 and, quite correctly, voted against it. However, if the Minister believes in the effectiveness of this board, would he answer the question as to why the period of exclusivity is retroactive for brand-name companies to June 27, 1986, but the retroactive provisions do not apply to the Drug Prices Review Board? Why the difference, if the Minister believes so sincerely in the Drug Prices Review Board?
Second, with respect to sales tax increases, can the Minister explain to Canadian consumers why $3 billion in additional sales taxes is good for the Canadian consumer, and I mean the increases of October 1, 1984 of $1 billion, on January 1, 1986, another $1 billion, and on April 1, 1986 another $1 billion? Would he also tell the House about the benefits to Canadian consumers in paying upwards of 23 cents a gallon more to drive their cars since 1984? Would he explain to Canadian consumers how this is of benefit to Canadian consumers?
Finally, while the Minister is on his feet, he ought not to misrepresent the suggestions that Members of Parliament have made. The Minister knows only too well that I have requested a copy of the CDIC report on the Principal Group. I am not suggesting, and the Minister knows that very well, that all confidentiality with regard to financial institutions be
breached. I have never suggested that. But I have said to the Minister that in this particular instance, because of 60,000 Canadians losing their life savings, is it not in the good public interest of this country that that be made public so Canadians can see the involvement of the federal Government? Thus far the Minister has said no, but I would like him to comment on that third point as well.

Mr. Speaker, the position of the Hon. Member on the question of CDIC and the Principal Group is a bit like trying to find a needle in a haystack. He says he is in favour of confidentiality but in this particular case he is not in favour of confidentiality. Is that what he is saying? What is the principle that guides the Hon. Member, the notoriety of a current predicament? Does that always override the principle of confidentiality?
I do not understand the Hon. Member's point. If he believes that confidentiality should be in place in some instances and not in others, could he tell me when he would discriminate against one and lean towards the other? My position is clear. There should be some confidentiality, but the CDIC should try to participate with information as much as it can, publicly and on a confidential basis, with inquiries such as the Code inquiry in Alberta.
Second, my understanding on the Drug Prices Review Board, and the Hon. Member can correct me if I am wrong, is that the Drug Prices Review Board is looking backward. It is not just looking forward. It is looking backward retroactively. I do not know where he gets that argument. I checked with the Minister before coming to the debate today. It is confirmed. It is looking backward as well as forward. Therefore, the point the Hon. Member makes is wrongly based unless I misunderstood the over-all thrust of what he was saying.
Finally, the Hon. Member asked about federal sales tax revenues in the last two or three years. A large part of those revenues has come from the growth of the economy which has led to increased revenues. This is the wonderful thing about growth, about jobs and about increasing investment. If one compares the period in office of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) from 1984 to 1988 with the period during which the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) was Minister of Finance, one will Find that revenues taken by the federal Government, proportionately, were much greater under that Liberal administration than they have been under this administration.
I really do not know the basis on which the Hon. Member has made his complaint about revenues. They are lower than they were under the Liberal administration of the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition when he was Minister of Finance, plus the fact that a large part of the increased take from federal sales tax comes from the growth of the economy.

Mr. Speaker, I was astonished to hear some of the statements made by the Minister. He suggested that provincial revenues had gone up very sharply in Manitoba and
March 24, 1988

that that was of itself wrong, ignoring the fact that under his own administration, federal revenues have gone up for a number of reasons, including substantial tax increases put into place by the Conservative Government. Those increases include three increases in sales tax, and sales tax revenues have in fact doubled under the Conservative Government since 1984.
I find the speciousness of the Minister's comments rather demeaning, and I am sorry to hear him make those particular comments. However, perhaps I can focus on a couple of things. In the first place, the Minister says he has not heard anything different from the New Democratic Party. The Liberals can speak for themselves with respect to economic policy, but what he has heard from the New Democratic Party is that we believe that full employment is as important an objective of economic policy as economic growth, the control of inflation and regional development. In fact, those things all fit together.
What has been lacking from the previous Government and from the present Government is, of course, a commitment to making full employment as important an objective as what the bankers, financiers and right-wing pundits tell the Government it ought to do.
Part of this resolution deals with the issue of bank charges. I listened with some concern to what the Minister had to say. He talked about great faith in the market system which brought us the crash last October. He talked about competition and he argued that the private sector was the engine of the economy. There is, in his view, no particular role for Government. I could contest that at some length, but what I would point to is his conclusion that this is the over-all answer to the concerns raised in the debate. For those consumers who have been concerned about bank charges, about the way they feel they have been victimized by increases up to 100 per cent in the last three or four years in charges levied by the bank for different services, his answer is: "Let them eat cake", because as far as he is concerned, the market system will short them out.
I suppose that I should applaud the courage of the Minister for sending out average consumers from coast to coast to do battle with Canada's multi-billion dollar banks and the banking system. Frankly, I think that is a rather unfair type of competition. If the Minister really cared about the consumer, he would be seeking to ensure that there was some force by which consumers acting collectively could receive a fair deal when the banks are ripping them off.

I am very happy to respond to the Hon. Member's points and questions, because I did not have an opportunity to elaborate further on the question of bank charges raised in the motion.
Bank charges are being looked at carefully by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. The Hon. Member is a member of that committee. I

am looking forward to that report. I would like to receive it quickly in order that we can act based upon it.
With that report in mind we will act, and the role of Government will be pivotal to the way we act. We will not leave it totally to competition. The Hon. Member knows that the competitive part of our answer to bank charges is an important part of the answer, but it is not the whole answer.
He is backing down, Mr. Speaker.
I am not backing down at all. The Government itself will have to act and it has acted before. There are a whole series of proposals-
This is like Saul on the road to Damascus.

-for disclosure, for elaborating on the role of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions with regard to regulating financial institutions. There is a superintendent not simply to keep competition buzzing along, which is great, but also to help to protect Canadians as consumers. As a matter of fact, the superintendent is doing an excellent job. We also have an interdepartmental committee looking at this before we receive the bank service report in order that we can respond very quickly when we receive the report. I think that the Member will be very happy with the way in which we will respond when we receive the report.
The role of the Government is essential in the protection of depositors and policy holders in a world where there is a market system or a centralized economy. It is absolutely central, and there is not very much difference about that. Where there is a difference of opinion between the Hon. Member and myself is in the importance of this new competition that I am insinuating into the system through our Blue Paper changes. Let me give the Hon. Member an example.
It was not too long ago that the big banks stated that they could not have variable rate mortgages. The Hon. Member knows something about mortgages. He has been involved in that issue. A humble trust company in my home town brought in variable rate mortgages. Three months later the banks found a way to bring in variable rate mortgages. A small trust company gave leadership to the whole system and the banks got on board. That is what we are going to bring into the economy, based on my reforms. After my reform is passed, insurance companies will be able to make consumer and commercial loans; trust companies over a certain size will have the total capacity to do the same. As a result, banks will have a great deal of competition. I know that that is not the total answer, but it is an important part of the answer for the Canadian consumer.

The Minister spoke at length on the tax reform. In the past three and a half years the Government has received from consumers more than $20 billion in taxes. Next week Canadian consumers will pay a one cent per litre tax increase on gasoline. Perhaps the Minister can tell us what that will do to the consumer.

My question is specifically related to the loss of value of properties due to the installation of supermailboxes. I am sure the Minister is aware of the Ontario Municipal Board ruling that supermailboxes installed in front of a house reduce its value. As a matter of fact, a citizen in the Municipality of Pickering had his or her property tax bill reduced because of that. Is this policy of the Government to stop delivering mail door-to-door to new subdivisions, and installing supermailboxes not affecting consumers at large? Canadians who invest their savings in a new home are now seeing values reduced because of the government policy of installation of supermailboxes. Not only do they receive second-class service, but also the value of their house and their investment is being reduced.

I am glad that the Hon. Member has interjected with this question. I feel very strongly about this whole question of postal service and the Canadian consumer. I know that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) does also.
If the price of stamps has to be doubled in order to have door-to-door delivery on a regular basis, the Canadian consumer will be up in arms. Our position is that the Canadian people want a responsible approach to Canada Post. They want postage stamps to be reasonably priced, and they want good service. When Canada Post reaches the stage of balancing its budget, which it will do shortly, we will then be in a position to make many choices on behalf of the consumer, such as, for example, if we want more service, if we want cheaper service, or if we want to make certain policy departures. The Government believes that those departures should not take place until the budget is balanced. The whole initiative of the Government on behalf of Canada Post has been excellent for the consumer.
In respect of the municipal example quoted by the Hon. Member, a reporter asked a resident of Pickering about this issue. I gather that it is the Town of Pickering that has decided to sue Canada Post and the federal Government for the use of supermailboxes. The following is what one resident, Muriel Beckett, had to say: "There are a lot of people around here that have a fire hydrant on their property. They have the electrical boxes too, so it is a trade-off. You get one or the other. I really don't think it will affect the property or the value of the property very much either".

speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. On debate, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre.

Mr. Speaker, time does not permit me to say all the things I would like to say in this debate over a very comprehensive, one might say unfocused, motion coming from the Liberals.
I note the double entente and the confusing messages delivered by the Government, as we witnessed in the speech given by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). He thumps himself on the chest and states that the private sector
is the engine of the economy. When one presses and starts to say that that engine is rolling over average Canadians, forcing people to the wall, and it is not being fair to poor consumers, suddenly the Minister states that we have to direct it a bit, and Government has to step in in order to play a role.
Most people who understand the Canadian economy know that we have a mixed economy in which there is an important role for the public sector, for the co-operative sector, and for the private sector. There is nothing wrong in saying that. But I find that this cant that comes forward from time to time from Progressive Conservatives is a little sickening. Generally, it seems to be directed at the New Democratic Party, a Party which has no problems at all in acknowledging that the private sector has a role, the public sector has a role, and there needs to be a co-operation between the different elements of our society if we are going to have a society which is just, equitable, effective, competitive, and fair to all of its citizens and residents.
I ask the Hon. Minister of State, does he really think that a society that is fair only to the rich and the powerful is the type of society Canadians want to achieve?
That is cant.

The Minister would say "No, of course not". He would state, "I want to be as fair to the widow in Newfoundland as to Conrad Black and to the other people who finance my Party in Toronto, and places like that".
In practice, the Government acts otherwise. That is one of the problems we have had with the Government over the last three or four years. That is not to say we did not have problems with the Liberal Party as well, and that the Liberal Party is not having its problems with itself. This resolution speaks to the inadequacies of postal service. It was the Liberal Party that created Canada Post, which is currently responsible for postal services. This resolution speaks to the high cost of gasoline. It was the Liberal Party that put the sales tax increase into the 1984 Budget which was implemented by this particular Government. The resolution speaks about the Government's acquiescence to sky-rocketing bank charges. That increase in bank charges did not begin after September 4, 1984; it began back in 1981 and 1982. Who was in power then? The Liberals were in power, Mr. Speaker.
The resolution also speaks to the unnecessarily high interest rate policy of the Government. I have challenged the Government on this issue. I have raised it again and again. However, let us not forget that 11 per cent mortgages are a heck of a lot better than the 19 per cent mortgages which prevailed when the Liberals were in power.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) ignored my question when I pointed out that he did not raise the interest rate issue in 1982 and 1983. It was the New Democratic Party which was raising the issue at that
March 24, 1988

time. Back-bench Liberals were mute while their own constituents were being forced out of business, were losing their homes, were losing their jobs, et cetera. I suppose time heals many things.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond agreed with me that interest rates were unnecessarily high six years ago, but then he said: "Well, we had a world recession at that time but we do not have a recession now". If we had a recession back then, what the devil was the Government doing imposing interest rates which the Liberal spokesperson on consumer affairs now admits were unnecessarily high? Why the devil did they not bring them down? I suppose that is a question which must be answered in the next election.
Also a question about economic and financial management needs to be raised, not just about the Conservative Party but about, the Hon. Minister of State for Finance will be glad to know, the Liberal Party itself. I should like to quote from Mr. Jeffrey Simpson's column today wherein he said: "The Liberals are stone broke. They face a deep and worsening financial crisis". He indicated that the Royal Bank, long a mainstay of the financial drives of the Liberal Party to maintain itself in power, has refused to extend its line of credit, and that the Liberal Party's corrective measures have invoked extreme controversy and differences of views within the Party to the point that the President of the Party is likely to be forced out, or forced to resign, or may in fact even lose a nomination. He also indicates that the Liberals are not yet sure how to get through the next six months without a crisis even more serious than the one of three weeks ago when the Party came within a whisker of not being able to meet its payroll.
The New Democratic Party has been giving a great deal of thought to how Canada needs to be governed and how the economy needs to be managed should we be called upon to form the Government after the next election. I want to say that a Party which does not even know how it can manage through the next six months is not displaying the necessary fitness to run the country again after the 1988 or 1989 election.
If I could turn my attention to the Minister of State for Finance, the Canadian Export Association and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association are increasingly raising questions about the high interest rate policy of the Government. Let us make no mistake that that is what we have. It was not created by the market system on its own. It was created by deliberate monetary policy being carried out by the Governor of the Bank of Canada and under the authority of the Government. The Government cannot wash its hands of that, because weekly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) meets with the Governor and he has the power to tell the Governor to bring down interest rates.
I am not sure whether or not the Governor blinked this week in terms of his annual report. He had the good grace not to mention zero inflation rates as his objective in his annual report. I thought there was some significance to that. He
Supply
indicated in his press conference that he was no longer prepared to confront or to seek confrontation with the Government in power. Nonetheless, we are also told that the Governor and the bank will continue to let interest rates rise on the treasury bill auction which they manage. Therefore they are bringing the bank rate up which, as the Minister of State for Finance knows, affects short-term interest rates in general and influences the inflow of money into the country.
Rather than acting, as the bank can, to bring interest rates down to a more reasonable level relative to world rates, particularly rates in the United States, the Bank of Canada is continuing to push up those rates. Instead, it is selling Canadian dollars wholesale in the exchange markets, to the point where we have doubled our foreign exchange reserves of U.S. dollars that have been tendered in return for Canadian dollars over the last year. By selling those Canadian dollars, the bank has prevented the exchange rate from going absolutely through the roof. However, now exporters are saying that it is bad enough at 80 cents because it is tougher for them to sell and to compete in Canada against imports. However, if the dollar goes up to 82, 83, or 84 cents, they will be facing a very serious situation.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association is now lending its voice to the concerns of New Democrats in saying, as I say now, that interest rates should be brought down by 1 per cent or more over a three-month period, a gradual decline which would allow for monitoring and adjustment if problems develop. I am pleased to have the support of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association on this particular question.
I point out to people who are in business and people who are concerned about Canada's trading relationship with the United States that in the course of just three months or four months we have seen an increase in the value of the Canadian dollar relative to the United States which has more than equalled the tariff cuts that the United States is committed to make over a 10-year period in the Canada-U.S. trade agreement signed last October.
If the trade agreement over 10 years is meant to be giving
100,000	or 150,000 jobs to Canada-and we do not know whether or not it is true-we will have a reverse move, which will lose 100,000 to 150,000 or more jobs to Canada, and all the benefit of the trade agreement will be wiped out. If the Government wants to be consistent, it should be keeping the dollar around 76 cents and moving ahead with the trade agreement. Instead, it gives with one hand, supposedly, and takes with the other, which can cause serious harm as far as the country is concerned.
A Government which is in fact concerned about the way in which a country is developing would look at the fact that the economy is somewhere at the full employment level in the area immediately around Metropolitan Toronto. There are jobs available; they are not necessarily good jobs, but there are jobs available. The unemployment rate is down to as low as 3 per cent to 4 per cent in certain areas. However, the idea expressed

by the Governor of the Bank of Canada that he must jam on the breaks every time the Toronto regional economy gets too hot seems to be unacceptable to average Canadians in most parts of Canada.
We should be talking about seeking means by which additional credit can be made available to areas like Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, northern British Columbia, and northern Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that in his attack on the banks, the Liberal Party critic chose to ignore the fact that his Party depends very heavily on contributions from the banking sector.
In 1984, donations to the Liberal Party by the banks equalled donations to the Conservative Party. The Bank of Montreal gave $75,000 to the Liberals; the Bank of Nova Scotia gave $70,000; the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce gave $70,000; the Royal Bank gave $75,000 to the Liberals; the Toronto-Dominion Bank gave $70,000; and the National Bank of Canada gave $30,000 in political donations to the Liberal Party of Canada.
In 1986, Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives received about $35,000 from each of the Big Five. The Liberals received $35,000 from the Bank of Montreal, $35,000 from the Bank of Nova Scotia, $37,000 from the Bank of Commerce, but apparently nothing from the Toronto-Dominion Bank and nothing from the Royal Bank. I imagine that was because they had gone too deeply into debt.
Mr. Speaker, we have here a Party that has remained friends with the banking sector. After all, the banks contributed $350,000 to the Liberal Party in 1984. Mr. Speaker, if they are returned to power, do you think the Liberal Party will stand up for the banks or for the average consumer? I think the answer is obvious.
I would like to deal with this question of bank charges. We are talking about a lot of money. In the last year for which we have figures, 1987, it is estimated that the direct bank charges for deposit accounts, safekeeping and payroll processing increased by about 20 per cent, to a total of $1.1 billion by the five chartered banks. If you bring in foreign exchange revenue, credit card fees, loan fees, securities commissions, bankers acceptances, letters of credit, guaranteed fees and other items, we are talking about a total of $4 billion which the banks collect annually. They are running amok in terms of the ways these fees have been increasing. For example, over the last five years, at a time when the economy was expanding at about 5 per cent and at a time when the banks were bringing in all kinds of new machinery to increase productivity, the Bank of
Commerce had a compound growth rate in its service charges to consumers of 17 per cent per annum. In 1983 it charged consumers $126 million, and in 1987 it charged them $235 million. The total of these fees now exceeds the profits that have been shown by the five chartered banks before the special provisions for Third World write-downs made back in 1987. This means that people are finding themselves paying every time they turn around at the chartered banks.
I have the figures here about increases in general for all the banks from 1982 to 1986. The Toronto-Dominion Bank increased its bank service charges by 75 per cent, the Royal Bank by 101 per cent, the Imperial Bank by 74 per cent, the Nova Scotia Bank by 81 per cent and the Bank of Montreal by 116 per cent.
If you look at the year over year increases for different services, Mr. Speaker, you will find that these charges are going up by 20 per cent, 30 per cent, 50 per cent or 100 per cent, and the consumer hardly knows where to turn or what he or she can do about it.
I have a letter here written to my friend, our spokesperson on unemployment insurance, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). This letter is from Winnipeg. It reads, in part, "Why was the bank deducting $1 off my account each month because the balance was below $200"? When the person went to the bank and asked it to do something, the bank said it would drop the charge if the person increased the balance in the account to over $200. Someone else was hit not once but twice for personalized cheques in one month just a few months ago. The cost was $8.06 a whack despite the fact that for years previously as a senior citizen, the person had never been charged for cheques. This person says, reflecting the anger existing out there-this is a senior citizen from Calgary, Alberta,-"the bastards are ripping me off'. This is somebody in their sixties or seventies. It is strong language but it shows how people feel about the treatment.
I have another example of cheques returned NSF. The service charge was $13.50 on a $75 cheque for Visa with the Bank of Commerce. A cheque for $50 was returned and a service charge of $13.50 was imposed. What it demonstrates, of course, is that if you are a small consumer then the charges are particularly onerous. If you are wealthy, you bounce a cheque and you pay $13, that is bad enough, but $13 on a $10,000 draft is something different than $13 on a cheque written for $50 or $100 by someone who has a very small income.
I think it is interesting to note in the figures that we have here just how much the cost of doing business can differ for a standard package of different services from different financial institutions. The Ottawa Citizen in January this year did an estimate and it found that the annual cost of a series of chequing and savings transactions for a typical Ottawa consumer would range from a low of $154 for someone at the CS Co-op up to $234 at the Scotia Bank; $258 at the Royal Trust and $276.20 at the Bank of Montreal. I bank with the
March 24, 1988

Bank of Montreal because it is close, by but perhaps I should reconsider that particular situation.
What I have found, and it makes me angry as a consumer myself, is that I get hit with these little charges here and there. It is $3 to put a cheque in on a monthly basis in order to keep my line of credit from getting out of sight. When I went to talk to the bank it said, "Oh, we are awfully sorry". The bank took the charge away. I am a Member of Parliament. I can find someone to talk to. The banks have to listen to me because they will possibly hear about the matter here in the House of Commons. But a constituent of mine living in Dalhousie ward is not in that position at all. A constituent of mine living in Dalhousie ward may feel that he or she has no choice but to spend as much as $20, $30 or $40 at a cheque cashing service because they cannot establish the ability to cash the cheque in a Canadian chartered bank. We have seen the collapse of the CCBs.
The Minister looks puzzled. The consumer protection agencies have been trying to bring this matter to the Minister's attention, but the Government has not been prepared to act on that front at all. That kind of action should be outlawed, and I believe that that should be a protection for the consumer. I believe that the chartered banks have the privilege to print money, the privilege to make billions of dollars in profits, the privilege to get by year after year without paying any tax at all, thanks to the privileges given to them by the Liberals and the Conservatives. The least the banks should be prepared to do is to cash a Government of Canada cheque or cash a welfare cheque from some average, ordinary Canadian or pensioner living on a small income and not force that person to go down that street to a cheque cashing service where he is ripped off, paying $5, $10, $25 to cash a cheque to put some bread on the table to feed the family or pay the rent.
That is reality and why I believe it is wrong, as the Minister said, to trust the market system alone. For God's sake this is a compassionate society, or it was until the Progressive Conservatives came to power. This is the Party that tried to deindex the old age pensions and tried to drive down the pensions of old age pensioners by 3 per cent year after year. This is the Party which deindexed the family allowances. In other words, it balanced its deficit not by taxing Conrad Black but by taking money away every month from families with children in this country. That is abject exploitation of average ordinary Canadians.
I realize, in talking about these things, that we are talking about the forthcoming election. In the forthcoming election I will be talking to my constituents in Ottawa Centre saying, "Do you want a Party that is prepared to give substantial tax cuts to only one group?" Only one group has tax cuts under tax reform, Mr. Speaker. The people who will be paying less in 1988 than in 1984 under the Conservative Government's tax reform are those with incomes of over $100,000 a year. The average family in my riding will be paying more than $1,000 in taxation after the Conservative Government tax reform than they were paying before. I am going to tell them that. No
Supply
doubt the Government will turn around and say, "Look at all the people we took off the tax rolls". But the Government forgets that these people were taken on the tax rolls first before they were taken off.
As far as my Party is concerned, we think that issues like this are substantive and important public issues. We believe that, yes, there is a cause and a case for Government to be involved in working at the social organization of our country to have a compassionate and a caring society. That is why we fought for medicare, full employment, hospital insurance, an adequate network of benefits for people who through bad luck cannot look after themselves. Most people really believe that. The banks should not be exempt from that.
I would like to see an ombudsman protect average Canadians in the banking system the way it is done in the United Kingdom. I would like to see local advisory committees established in every community with whom the banks would have to consult from time to time on the nature of their services. I would like to see a government prepared to stand up for average Canadians and not just for wealthy Canadians.

subsubtopic: LATVIA-CEREMONY SCHEDULED TO COMMEMORATE VICTIMS OF STALINIST DEPORTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a ceremony will be held in Latvia tomorrow, March 25, to remember the victims of Stalinist deportations. The Helsinki '86 Human Rights Group of Latvia has called on all Latvian citizens to commemorate victims of the mass deportations of 1949 by laying flowers at the Statue of Liberty in Riga at 1830 hours, that is 10.30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, tomorrow.
On March 25, 1949, a mass round-up began resulting in the deportation of over 43,000 individuals from Latvia. The action was part of Stalin's forced collectivization by the physical removal of independent farmers and destruction of the traditional rural base of the country. These mass deportations, which struck all three Baltic States simultaneously, were considerably larger than those of June 14, 1941, commemorated this past summer. If indeed the U.S.S.R. authorities allow the ceremony in Riga to proceed peacefully tomorrow, we will have seen a concrete example of glasnost.

Mr. Speaker, on November 9, 1987, the Polish Government arrested and imprisoned Dr. Kornel Morawiecki, leader of the Polish Opposition Group "Solidarnosc Walczaca", or "Fighting Solidarity", a non-violent underground organization.
Morawiecki had been in hiding since the imposition of martial law in 1981. During the last six years he devoted his
energy to the creation of this movement whose goals are democracy, freedom, and respect for human rights. The only crime of this brave Polish patriot is his dedication and commitment to the pursuit of these goals, and his unlawful arrest is clearly a violation of the letter and spirit of the Helsinki Accord to which Poland and Canada are both signatories.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Government of Canada to use every means at their disposal to secure the release of Kornel Morawiecki from his illegal imprisonment.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) is undermining and discrediting Canada's refugee status determination system and our legal obligations to the UN. Last week the Minister moved to deport 40 Turks out of the backlog of 46,000 refugee claimants, whereas this week the same Minister indicated he is prepared to start a new administrative review to clear the backlog. It is grossly unjust to deport some now and later allow others to stay through administrative review.
Today we learn the Minister will in a few weeks fire about 10 of the most highly qualified and competent members of the Refugee Status Advisory Committee. Among them are Susan Davis, formerly a protection officer in Canada with the UN High Commission for Refugees; William Barton, former Canadian Ambassador to the UN and liaison with the UNHCR; and Yvon Beaulne, formerly Canadian Ambassador with experience in the UNHCR. Such people have proven expertise and judgment in refugee matters. They are being dumped, evidently to be replaced by Tory hacks who will assist the Minister to expel refugees. Shame on the Government for its campaign against refugees.
