speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express concern about the manner in which applications for Canada Pension disability benefits are processed. They are rejected at the first level as a matter of course and further appeals are very time consuming and frequently result in injustices to claimants. I am advised that the text outlined in the Act is the source of the problem, but that is only partly the case. The process is also faulty.
I therefore urge the Minister to consider changing the test prescribed in the Act so that disabled Canadians unable to work may receive the benefits to which they feel entitled. I also urge that an end be put to the routine rejection of applications at the lower level of assessment. It is time for this unworkable legislation and process to be changed.

subtopic: BILL C-85-USE OF PROVISIONS AGAINST NON-STRIKING WORKERS
BILL C-85-USE OF PROVISIONS AGAINST NON-STRIKING WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to tell Hon. Members of the unfortunate and unwanted
consequences resulting from the passage by this House last August of Bill C-85 which ordered striking railway workers back to work.
This legislation is now being used by the CPR to intimidate non-striking workers by the threat of fines of up to $1,000 a day if they refuse to cross picket lines. The CPR uses those provisions written into Bill C-85 as a way to intimidate its workers regardless of their collective bargaining situation.
There is no great emergency facing the railways today. There is no certainty that non-striking workers will be fined for refusing to cross the picket lines of a legal strike. The only certainty is that the CPR is using any means it can to keep operating.
This is a clear CPR strategy to divide its work force. It won't work, but the House of Commons should realize that this action is a direct result of the use and misuse of the passage of Bill C-85.

subtopic: LANGUAGE TEACHERS-REQUEST THAT LABOUR CONFLICT BE RESOLVED
LANGUAGE TEACHERS-REQUEST THAT LABOUR CONFLICT BE RESOLVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that, after 18 months, the employees of the Education Group of the Public Service Alliance of Canada are still in conflict with the Treasury Board.
The last meeting between management and the union was held on January 13, 1988, and nothing has happened since. This group of federal Government employees has been without a contract for 18 months, since September 1986. What is at issue is not money or wages, but the work load of the teachers.
Under the terms of the Government offer, language teachers could spend 37 1/2 hours a week teaching for 20 consecutive weeks without any time allowed during their workday for course preparation. Under these conditions, Mr. Speaker, the quality of the teaching and the performance of the teachers would certaintly deteriorate. We have to wonder whether the Conservative Government has a hidden agenda as concerns the teaching of our official languages.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs. Last July the Government of Canada signed a memorandum of understanding with the Government of Newfoundland. Perhaps I could get the attention of the Minister of Justice because this is also a question of justice.
The memorandum of understanding that was signed with regard to the Inuit land claims has still not gone to the federal Cabinet. If the Minister of Indian Affairs is serious about giving native people more self-government, why has it not gone to Cabinet? Why is he holding up the land claims negotiations? When will he start giving them more self-government and more self-determination?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of the Western Diversification Office; Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: LABRADOR 1NUIT LAND CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's concern on behalf of his constituents. The Province of Newfoundland, as of early January or late December past, brought out its comprehensive claims policy. I have asked for and received clarification of that policy.
I have had discussions with the Government of Newfoundland and with the Labrador Inuit as to their impression of the policy and we are hoping to be able to reach an agreement and proceed with the mandate. Once the mandate and the bilateral issues have been decided between the province and the ILA, we will be able to proceed with negotiations.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not only has there been no information coming from the Government of Canada but there has

March 24, 1988
Oral Questions
been no consultation from the Government of Newfoundland, as I understand it. The Labrador Inuit have nothing on paper with regard to the memorandum of understanding between the two Governments or consultation with the province.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate to condemn the Government's policy with respect to the Canada Post Corporation.
During the past two years, Canada Post has increased the price of stamps twice, had two postal strikes and may possibly have a third, and has substantially reduced services, thus creating two classes of citizens in Canada: those who get their mail delivered at home and those who have to brave the elements and go to the infamous superboxes to pick up their mail.
The problem is a Conservative Government that has reversed the mandate and priorities of Canada Post. This Government is to blame for the disastrous state of our postal services today.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is a good country to live in, but it is a vast territory that often defies the laws of nature and reason, and a country rich in cultural, linguistic and regional diversity. To stress the need for satisfactory communications, it is often said Canada was built along its railways. In fact, at the time of Confederation, Mr. Speaker, when we became a nation, the Government set itself two goals: To protect and defend our country and to deliver the mail.
Of course, this was in 1867, and at the time, communications went by mail. Since then, technology has made spectacular progress, but the fact remains that postal services are still essential to all citizens of this country.
I don't think there is any question about it. Everyone realizes that public transit is an essential service, although many people never take the train or the bus. But everybody gets mail, Mr. Speaker.
In 1981, when the Liberal Government set up the Canada Post Corporation, it recognized that the postal service is an essential service. It is not a whim nor a luxury but a basic service to be made available to all Canadians.
Therefore, it is in that spirit that the Government had given Canada Post a mandate including three equally important aspects as follows: first, Mr. Speaker, to stabilize relations between employer and unions; secondly, to improve the postal service and thirdly to reduce the deficit.
From 1981 to 1984, Canada Post Corporation adequately carried out its mandate. It took some steps forward in reducing

March 24, 1988
Supply
its deficit. It improved labour relations. The Liberal Government appointed union representatives to the board of directors to provide a link between the Corporation and the workers and to promote social peace. That is the problem at the Canada Post Corporation. The situation has reached a point where if an employee forgets to punch out at noon, he is suspended three days without pay. The incredible fact, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government has exerted so much pressure on the Canada Post Corporation that the employees are no longer inclined to work. Such is the basic problem and this why we expect that the mail will not be delivered on time, Mr. Speaker ...
Therefore, the Liberal Government had then recognized that a coalition should exist between employer and unions, that an efficient management was necessary to give a better service to Canadians and we did so.
During the 1984 election, the Conservatives promised the moon, but once in power they threw off the disguise. They became true Conservatives over again and started slashing services. In this way, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in 1986 decided that for Canada Post Corporation the priority was no longer to deliver the mail, but to balance the books in no time, whatever the impact on service.
In the United States, Mr. Speaker, they took 14 years to balance the books. Here in Canada, a country as vast as ours, with our kind of remote areas and a small population, we want to reduce the Post Office's deficit over five years. Unbelievable, Mr. Speaker! That approach is not rational, and Canadians have to pay for it.
When Canada Post Corporation was established, the Liberal Government had a policy of offering community letterbox service to residents in new projects until home delivery was available. It was a temporary service that in no case was to become permanent. But in 1985 a Conservative Government, anxious to cut costs at any price, forced Canada Post Corporation to permanently set up the superbox system.
This means that since 1985, no new homes got home delivery nor have any hope of ever getting it. In 1986, following the Minister of Finance's statement, the Government just created two classes of citizens: one that gets home delivery and another that must go fetch their mail in a box. By 1991, Mr. Speaker, nearly one million homes and two million Canadians will be served by superboxes. But those superboxes are a second-rate service for second-rate citizens. How can the Government force an 80-year-old widow to get out at minus 20, 30 or 40 degrees temperatures to go and fetch, in a frozen superbox that will not open, an Old Age Security pension cheque that may not even be there because oftentimes postmen, on account of the snow, cannot deliver the mail. Mr. Speaker, this is unfair, irrational and discriminatory.
In the case of rural areas, the Government also intends to use collective mailboxes at major intersections and to close about 5,000 rural post offices within the next five years. What a lack of vision, Mr. Speaker, what a lack of understanding of
the community fabric of Canada! Everyone knows that the post office is still a gathering place in our villages and small towns. It often becomes an information centre for all citizens. It is where people go to look for social services and to ask for information on such matters as tax returns, scholarships and job applications; the postmaster often becomes a resource person. The federal Government is present everywhere, and the post office remains a familiar place where the Government takes on human dimensions. It creates a link with the community. It is a unifying force which gives a feeling of belonging to the community and to each of its members.
What I am telling you, Mr. Speaker, is not romanticism or poetry or a politician's dreams, but the basic truth. As evidence of that fact, I have here a letter sent to the president of the Canada Post Corporation by the mayor of the small community of Trinity Bay, and with your permission, I would like to quote from it. The mayor of Trinity Bay says: "If the few businesses which we have and on which we rely for our survival stay here, it is because we have services such as the post office. Centralization for economy's sake must not be pushed to such an extent that it jeopardizes the existence of small communities ... We urge you to find means to keep our post office, even if doing so would mean sharing with others certain of the most costly aspects of the postal service. For us here, sharing is a matter of survival, and we know something about it. For God's sake, do not help to destroy us!"
Mr. Speaker, Trinity Bay is certainly not important for the powerful Conservative Government, but we, Liberals, are well aware of the fact that there are thousands of communities like Trinity Bay in Canada. Indeed, over 2,500 communities in Canada do not even have a bank, only a post office. How can there be any thought of removing this link with the rest of the country? We, Liberals, understand that it is our duty to protect the character and the way of life of these communities and to serve them adequately. The Conservatives are obsessed by the Canada Post Corporation. Yet, it costs less to operate it than other Crown corporations of the same size, 60,000 employees.
In 1985-86, the Government paid to the Canada Post Corporation $180 million, or 6.2 per cent of its operation budget. Never, since the establishment of the Canada Post Corporation, has the Government provided it with more than 12 per cent of its budget.
In fact, over a three year period, more specifically from 1982 to 1985, the Government's share of its financing was reduced from 10.3 per cent to 6.3 per cent. This represents quite a valuable improvement, especially at a time when services are being increased instead of cut.
The Minister claims that home delivery would cost $1.3 billion and that to maintain it, the cost of a single stamp would have to be increased to 60 cents. The Minister is grossly exagerating, for according to Canada Posts' own data, $500 million-these are the figures for 1988-over a five year
March 24, 1988

period would be enough to replace the superboxes with home delivery.

Yesterday we read in the newspapers that the Post Office is set to double the supermailboxes. "Canada Post plans to resume the installation of its controversial supermailbox in the hopes to nearly double their number by the end of the summer". Then we hear that: "Town plans to launch suit after supermailbox cut". The Ontario Municipal Board recognized that a supermailbox installed in front of a home reduced the value of the property and the municipality reduces the tax bill. Now the municipality wants to sue the federal Government for its loss of tax revenue. What are the savings of the federal Government in installing the famous supermailboxes?

Mr. Speaker, the Canada Post Corporation must fully assume its mail delivery mandate. It is the Government's responsibility to re-establish the mandate of 1981 which included improving its labour relations, increasing its productivity and reducing its deficit.
Canadian men and women want their mail to be delivered to their door every day of the week. They want an efficient and unified service which is the same for everybody. What would people say about a postman who would deliver the mail only on one side of the street? That is exactly what this Tory Government is trying to do. In my own riding, there are people living on one side of the street who are having their mail delivered at home, while those on the other side must get them from the superboxes. Yet, these people pay the very same taxes. Which proves that the Government has created with these superboxes two classes of citizens not for a little while, but for ever and ever.
Canadian men and women want also to keep their rural post offices open because they feel they are practical and useful, and because they are part of the social communication network of their community. We also want to keep the rural post offices open, because they represent a privileged link with citizens who are often isolated.
Instead of closing the post offices, the Government should enhance them by offering consumers postal related products such as greeting cards, correspondance and wrapping paper.
In Canada, Mr. Speaker, all citizens worthy of the name are first class citizens. We are all equal. We pay the same taxes. We all have to buy a 37 cents stamp to send a letter. We are all entitled to the very same services, including mail services.
Of course, we all agree on the need to balance the budgets, whether it is that of the Canada Post Corporation or of any other organization. But the way to do that is not to reduce services or raise the price of a stamp to 60 cents, as the Minister claims. Management has to be creative, dynamic and competitive, they have to come up with novel and modern ways to boost revenues.
Supply
Studies have revealed that Canada Post would considerably increase its revenues simply by advertising on its trucks or at post office entrances. Some people claim that commercial advertising would tarnish the corporate image of Canada Post, but this is a specious argument because public transit systems have shown that trucks, buses or shelters can carry advertising without having a negative impact on the corporate image.
It is simply a matter of making sure that such advertising is in keeping with clear and relevant quality standards.
Private sector interests are acutely aware of post office goodwill and they know this is the way to boost their sales.
Mr. Speaker, the Government rejects progress. It rejects dynamism and fresh ideas. Its only solution is to reduce services. How can anyone be so blind?
Everywhere else in the world they find new ways to continue to serve people. Here in Canada the only way we have to solve these problems is to reduce services.
We must also set our sights on new technologies, new services which are getting ever more profitable such as electronic mail and mail advertising or direct mail.
According to a study by McLeod, Young & Weir, Canada is now eight years behind the United States in the use of sophisticated forms of direct mail.
In that case, the volume of direct mail handled by Canada Post will have to increase by about 115 per cent annually over the next eight years in order to reach the present level of distribution per capita in the United States.
By the same token, this would mean an impressive increase of revenues from third class mail. Indeed, from $300 million that it is now, Canada Post could increase its turnover in that area to $600 million. That is an extra $300 million annually. That in itself would be enough to balance the books at Canada Post Corporation, get rid of superboxes, keep our rural post offices and deliver the mail to all Canadians on time.
That is, Mr. Speaker, what should be done to settle those problems once and for all. I am glad to see the Minister in the House and I hope he will give some consideration to my comments and sit down with Canada Post Corporation to settle these problems once and for all.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) deserves our thanks and congratulations for the remarkable account he just gave of this very serious problem.
I wish as well to pay tribute to him for all the work he has accomplished these past few months regarding this important issue.
Furthermore, it is worth pointing out what seems a rather unusual and all the more positive element, in that in his speech, the Member also suggested some solutions, some answers to the problem.

Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I must add that I, myself, have had repeated opportunities to realize, in my own riding, the extreme importance of door-to-door daily mail delivery. I even decided for the sake of experience to follow in the steps of the rural postman during a few days, while he delivered his mail along concession roads, some very remote, and in the small towns vicinity, only to find out that as soon as he leaves an envelope or a newspaper in the mailbox, it is a matter of seconds before they are picked up. Not too many such experiences are required to understand how essential this service simply is and to know that cutting or reducing it would bring some very drastic consequences. And here, 1 am not particularly referring to elderly people.
The question I would like to ask my colleague is this: I know that he is an accountant. I am also aware that in his trade, anything called a deficit is obviously a matter of great concern. I also know that he has carried out several studies on the subject and I ask him the following questions: Does he think it possible not only to not cut services but to increase them and still make profits or at least enable the Corporation to balance its budget?
What we have seen for some months is the creation of a whole series of new businesses which I assume are making astronomical profits delivering mail.
Thus, in the light of all that, I ask my colleague if, according the him, Canada Post Corporation can balance its budget while maintaining and enhancing its present services in some other areas.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my colleague for his compliments and his question. Mr. Speaker, because we are limited I ran out of time and I was unable to deliver part of my speech.
Last January, Mr. Speaker, Revenue Canada advised all employers that as of January this year any remittance of payroll deductions bearing a postage stamp dated the fifteenth and arriving one or two days after will not be considered and therefore a penalty will be imposed pursuant to the Revenue Canada statute.
Now in answer to the question of my colleague, yes, Canada Post can continue to provide essential services, keep rural post offices open, and deliver mail at the door instead of through superboxes without unduly increasing postage, and all this is possible, Mr. Speaker, because good service will definitely increase the volume of business, as we saw in the latest financial statement for 1986. There were no strikes between 1981 and 1986, so both revenues and business volume went up. In other words, the business community and people generally had begun to rely on Canada Post.
But then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) gave out his marching orders: the purpose of the whole exercise is not to provide better service or improve labour relations but to cut down the deficit, period. As a result of these orders the climate
and service automatically deteriorated, and we are definitely going to pay for that because revenues will now begin to go down.

I wish to take part briefly in this discussion with the Hon. Member regarding postal service, and his particular reference to the supermailboxes. By way of a brief preamble, I was wondering why the Hon. Member ignores what is largely a suburban reality in many parts of the country. If one looks at the demography and the working trends in urban Canada today, I wonder as most responsible people should in this debate, if one has door-to-door delivery in those brand new subdivisions, how many people are at home at 9.30 or 9.45 in the morning to pick up mail, cheques, and valuable correspondence that would otherwise be left in the mailbox beside the door for the rest of the day? Is the proposition that people should walk 600 feet to a supermailbox to pick up their mail, an impossible task for the demography of the new suburban neighbourhoods which are usually young, working couples? One should also look at the fact that this is not a deprivation of service; these are subdivisions that were not there before. They often and usually have young couples who are moving into or building a new home.
In 1977 when I lived in Saskatoon, all the new subdivisions, under the former Liberal Government, did not have door-to-door delivery extended. In 1977 the Liberal Government stated that the cost to do this was clearly excessive to Canada Post.
In light of the millions of dollars that it would cost to extend door-to-door delivery in new suburbs, in light of the fact that supermailboxes are a secure way of having mail service in new subdivisions, which is exactly what happens in the small town where I live, where we always have to go to the Post Office to use our lock boxes and in light of the fact that to provide door-to-door delivery would result in a stamp costing approximately 65 cents, I wish to ask the Hon. Member if he can assure people in my constituency that the Liberal Party would indeed restore full door-to-door delivery at a cost of millions of dollars and at a cost of a 65-cent stamp. Would the Member give us an answer? I know his time is drawing short. It need not be a long answer. The question simply is, will the Liberal Party in the next election state that it will provide door-to-door delivery to all new subdivisions? Yes or no.

I know that my time is short, but I wish to say that the Hon. Member outdid the Minister because the Minister mentioned a 60-cent stamp and the Hon. Member is now up to 65 cents. I do not know if the Hon. Member is doing better or worse, but I hope that he checks his figure. Each day it increases by five cents.
I wish to correct the record. The Hon. Member was talking about the Liberal policy in 1977. It was in 1974 that the policy was clear on the communities-

You are skating on awfully thin ice.

If you listen carefully perhaps you will learn something. Communities with 2,000 or more points of call always received door-to-door mail delivery. One only has to come to my riding and check the records. A future Liberal Government, yes, will return to the policy of giving Canadians door-to-door mail service for communities with 2,000 or more points of call. That was the previous policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear the hon. spokesman for the Liberal Party talk about the commitment of the Liberal Party to door-to-door delivery for communities with 2,000 doors or more. What the Hon. Member is saying is that the Liberal Party agrees with this second-class policy. There will be two classes of Canadians, those who live in communities of 2,000 or more who will receive door-to-door service, and second-class citizens, according to how the Liberals describe the class of citizens, of people who do not live in those communities. What is so wonderful about that division? What will the Liberals do to those who live in a community of 1,950 doors? They will say: "That's too bad. You are second-class, you are not going to get door-to-door delivery". That is the absurdity of the type of statement made by the Hon. Member.
The Party with which the Hon. Member is aligned, when it was in power and when the Post Office was not a Crown corporation but a Department of Government, put a freeze on door-to-door delivery. It was done for a very good reason, because the world is changing. When I grew up there was door-to-door milk and bread delivery. Shopping was basically done on foot. Corner grocery stores were everywhere for one to purchase one's groceries. In those days something less than 20 per cent of married women worked. The family and the living circumstances were entirely different than today. Today, in the majority of families, both spouses work. The living style is to have two cars, to live in the suburbs, which is the areas wherein people are serviced by group mailboxes. The pattern is that there are not even sidewalks in recognition of the fact that people travel by car and park in the driveway or garage. They shop in the evenings in shopping centres. The Post Office is changing its delivery methods to reflect that new reality.
It strikes me as being a little ironic that the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party consider themselves the more progressive parties. They call us the "dinosaurs". We are prepared to acknowledge that society is changing and that that should be acknowledged in the services. These "progressive" Parties say: "No, no, no. If it was good enough in the 1940s and 1950s, it is good enough today. No change. Keep it the way it is". They are the reactionaries. Their policy on the Post Office is to go back to the days when we lived on streets that had sidewalks and narrow lots, and when mama stayed home.
Supply
Let us go back to those days and let us not go forward to the new era. That is fine. If they as Parties wish to project to the people of Canada that it is their intention to have door-to-door delivery, or to instruct the Crown corporation to do that, then in all fairness they have to answer the question as to where the money will come from.
The fact is that five years is the period of the corporate plan. To bring in door-to-door delivery to every home now serviced by group mailboxes-and we are not talking about rural routes or general delivery-over the next five years, the fact is that it would cost an additional $1,300 million and thereafter $400 million per year in operating costs. The figures are there.
It is all well and good to sit in opposition and say: "What is $400 million or $ 1 billion compared with the potential votes we can get by making this promise?" They can sit there and say: "It is peanuts. What we are talking about here is votes. We don't worry about silly little things like $1 billion or $400 million per year of extra costs".
Well, that translates into a 60-cent stamp. An Hon. Member was saying that the Post Office should look for a growth in business. How would it grow in business if it raises the cost of a stamp to 60 cents? Just normal economics tells us that if it raises the cost of delivering a letter, it will have less letters to deliver. According to Economics 101, raise the price and demand goes down. One does not get more business by raising the price; one gets less business.
It is an irresponsible suggestion. I can understand that it is tempting. We have unions out there funding organizations such as RAM, Residents Against Mailboxes, which are petitioning and invoking images of elderly and handicapped people struggling through snowdrifts trying to get to their mailboxes to pick up the mail and being denied the luxury of having mail put into the boxes on the sides of their houses. They are traditional techniques used in politics, propaganda techniques, but I think one would underestimate the intelligence of Canadians to play that card too frequently and with too much prominence.
I think Canadians realize that the world is changing. I think anybody who looks around at our society recognizes that if you do not get milk delivery or door-to-door bread delivery nowadays, you have to find some way to get your groceries and it is not too difficult at the same time to get your mail. Indeed, the Post Office has a policy for the handicapped or people who are simply unable to leave their homes. In fact they can arrange to have door-to-door delivery. Again I do not think those images invoked in the propaganda war will be too believable.
If the Liberal Party wants to put forward the proposal that it is preferable to spend that extra money, $400 million per year, in order to have door-to-door delivery everywhere, if that is its priority, I think it is legitimate to put it to the people of Canada and let them decide. However, it is not legitimate to

March 24, 1988
Supply
suggest that somehow it can be done with no cost, that somehow we can wave a wand and make it disappear because we cannot. There is no such thing as a free lunch. It has to be paid for.
If it is the decision of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party that rather than spend $400 million on day care, education, or science and technology, those resources or that amount of money is better spent on door-to-door delivery of mail, that is their decision. They should put it before the people in all honesty and let them decide. This is what democracy is all about. However, to try to imply that there is no cost associated with these promises is dishonest at the least. As I indicated, it assumes a degree of ignorance on the part of the people of Canada which I do not believe is there. They will be able to see through that kind of posturing and behaviour.
The motion with which we are dealing today is a real potpourri. It sounds like the Hon. Member for Cape Breton- East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) is blaming the Government of Canada for everything from poor postal services, to high prescription drugs, to the cost of gasoline, to acne. I understand that there is an outbreak of chicken pox in the day care centre in the Confederation Building. I guess that must be the Government's fault too and should be included in the motion! They seem to think that everything they deem to be wrong with Canadian society is due to the Government.
When we talk about the Post Office, one gets the impression sometimes from listening to the Opposition that until September, 1984 Canada Post was one of the best, smoothest running organizations in the world, certainly in Canada. One gets the impression that the mail got through on time all the time, that everybody got door-to-door delivery, that labour relations were sweet, that everything was hunky-dory, and that it all fell apart in September, 1984 when we were elected to Government. Of course that is absurd. In 1983 the Post Office was running a deficit of $500 million. It was borrowing $500 million. It is still there in the debt. It kept borrowing in those days. It will be paid for by future generations. The Liberal policy was very simple- "Let future generations pay for the cost of delivering a letter today". That was the kind of deficit in 1983, and all people did not get door-to-door delivery; a $500 million deficit and no door-to-door delivery in new suburbs.
Some progress has been made. This coming fiscal year the Post Office will make a profit for the first time since 1971-72. It will be a small profit but a profit. Productivity has been going up for the last three years in the Post Office at the rate of 3.5 per cent per year. Business has increased by 23 per cent. Indeed, the over-all expenditures of the Post Office over the last couple of years, and projected into next year, have increased as a result of three roughly equal measures: There has been a business increase, more volume; there has been an increase in the cost of stamps less than the cost of inflation; and there has been an increase in productivity. The Post Office is more efficient. It is making significant progress, and an honest Member of Parliament would acknowledge that.
Is there a lot left to be done? Yes, indeed there is, but current management is working on it. If only we could stop beating on them through this political process, stop the immature games that are being played at the political level all the time, and give them an opportunity to continue to make progress, we might see the day where this Crown Corporation was viewed by the majority of Canadians as one which is providing a good service at reasonable cost. It is a fair thing and a possible thing to look forward to. However, the temptation to play political games, make wild accusations, and so on is simply too overwhelming for too many people.
I guess that I am running out of time, but I would like to deal very briefly with one issue raised by the sponsor of the motion today, the one concerning prescription drug prices. Bill C-22, which we finally got through Parliament after the greatest of resistance by the Opposition Parties, is in place and is paying off. I have a little 20-page brochure here talking about the research and development commitments that have already resulted from Bill C-22-hundreds of millions of dollars. Today there are thousands of young Canadian scientists working as a result of Bill C-22, and Bill C-22 has not caused the increase in the price of any drug in Canada by a single penny. Anybody who claims otherwise is not telling the truth or is ignorant, not telling the truth because they are lying or not telling the truth because they are ignorant. However, such is the case of these people who were bitter about losing this battle. They keep raising these phoney studies about supposed price increases. We had one the other day from a couple of pharmacists from Toronto who said that the price of drugs had risen. The Toronto Star featured the study. The matter was raised in the House. A Senator raised it in the other place. Accusations were made; for instance, that Bill C-22 has caused the price of drugs to rise.
The study is a very interesting one. First it made comparisons by using last year's wholesale price versus this year's retail price. It looked at last year's price without federal tax versus this year's price with federal tax. It looked at drugs that were wholly manufactured in Switzerland and Germany. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Swiss franc and the German mark have gone up in value relative to the Canadian dollar. The study recommended that people look at the outrageous increase in price. In terms of the Swiss franc and the German mark, there was no increase whatever. Because of currency changes there was an increase in Canadian dollars, but none of this has anything to do with the patent system or Bill C-22 which changed the patent system. But that does not stop these lovers of truth and honesty from blaming currency changes on Bill C-22. It is absolute absurdity.
I can understand a political arena where from time to time people do things like that. It is less understandable to see some of these guardians of truth in information dissemination in the fourth estate making these kinds of claims in print as some,
March 24, 1988

only some, did, Mr. Speaker. That is less acceptable but again it is something that we need to deal with.
I guess the ultimate absurdity is the failure to acknowledge that if the opposition had not delayed the Bill, filibustered it or had not played silly games, we would now have in place the Drug Prices Review Board. The board would have the capability of looking at prices of all drugs and making reasonable and rational assessments as to whether price increases were appropriate or not appropriate and could take remedial action or exercise downward pressure on companies that might attempt to introduce drug prices in excess of the cost of living.
To do everything possible to delay the implementation of that Drug Prices Review Board and then to scream bloody murder when the Drug Prices Review Board is not there to me is hypocrisy at the least, if not worse. I could go on. Perhaps it is unnecessary because one of the great things about being a Canadian with our well educated and intelligent population is the comfort it gives in knowing that by and large people can see through most of this nonsense. Even when you have Members of the Opposition making crazy claims about Bill C-22 and about post office costs, supermailboxes and so on, in the end the public is intelligent enough to see the accusations for what they are, propaganda at best and outright deceit at worst perhaps. Since people can see through that, it is not that much of a concern on the part of the Government. It is something we need not get overly concerned about. While a motion like this gives us an opportunity to fill a day's debate in the House of Commons, nobody is fooled by the nonsense indicated in the motion.

Mr. Speaker, would the Hon. Minister give me an answer to a question which my constituents frequently ask? I have several thousand new homes in the suburban part of my constituency. Many of the residents in these new homes call or come to me and say: "Before I lived in this new home in the suburbs where I have to get my mail from the supermailboxes, I lived in an older part of your constituency and I was getting door-to-door delivery. I moved into this new house in an urban area. The house costs more, it is worth more than the old house and I am paying much higher municipal taxes than I did before. My wife and I are working. We are paying much more in income tax than we did before. Why can I not get the same door-to-door mail service as I did when I lived in the old part of Winnipeg? Why am I treated as a second class citizen?" Frankly, I have no answer for them. I would like to be able to tell the people how the Minister would answer that question. Why do we have two classes of citizens in the cities of Canada, class one which gets door-to-door service and class two which has to depend on supermailboxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, actually there are four classes. First, you have classes of citizens who pick up their mail at general delivery in urban environments or in rural environments, small towns and villages. You have classes of citizens who go to the post office to pick up their mail at lock boxes.
Supply
You have classes of citizens who get their mail through rural route delivery systems. There are classes of citizens who get their mail door-to-door and you have classes of citizens who get their mail through group mailboxes. That situation has been in place for over 100 years, since the Post Office has been in existence. There has never been a time in the history of the Post Office whereby the majority of people got door-to-door delivery. It was always a minority of people who received postal services door-to-door. There is a bit of an illusion that somehow we are changing from what had been an historic situation. It is not true.
The Hon. Member talked about the difference between the downtown older neighbourhood and the new suburban areas.
Not downtown.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
We have changed patterns. The older neighbourhoods built in the 1940s and 1950s was at a time when mostly the wife did not work but stayed home. If there was a car in the family, that was all there was, public transport was used and the way of living was different. Most streets had sidewalks. People walked a lot. Shopping was done at local stand alone stores and shops.
It may have escaped the notice of the Hon. Member, but in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s things changed. Shopping centres came into existence. New suburbs opened up. Lots were bigger. People moved to the suburbs for the benefit of a bigger backyard. Most of these neighbourhoods do not have sidewalks because people do not walk. We see mainly two car families now. Shopping is done at shopping centres where people buy their groceries, pick up their dry cleaning, and it is done in the evening. Both partners work in most families now. We have changed. The world has changed.
The Post Office was trying to change in keeping with those changing patterns. The Hon. Member is suggesting that what was good for the 1940s and 1950s, and the lifestyle that most Canadians lived in those days ought to be retained for the 1980s and 1990s. For a reactionary like the Hon. Member, I can understand that, but the fact that the Post Office will adjust and adopt to modern lifestyles and the way we live today should not be viewed as such a shocking and terrible thing. It is certainly inaccurate to describe this situation as having first class and second class citizens in it. There has always been several ways of delivering the mail. There is today. There has been those differences for over 100 years. Undoubtedly there will continue to be in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister a question, but before I do, I would like to tell him that perhaps he was on the opposition benches for too long. He was playing the kind of game that he accuses us of playing now when he was in Opposition. I would like to remind him that his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), said before the election that he would never increase taxes, that increasing taxes would be wrong. Indeed, in three and a half years, the

Minister of Finance took away over $22 billion in taxes from consumers.
During Question Period this afternoon, the Minister was temporarily absent, so I asked the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) if the Minister could release the figures he was talking about to justify the $ 1.3 billion cost to Canada Post. I called Canada Post and was told that in 1986 figures, it would cost $360 million and in 1988 figures, $500 million for a five-year period. Who is telling the truth here?
Why does the Minister not defend his own figures by releasing them so that Members of the House and Canadians in general could know exactly what he is talking about? Why is he talking about a 60-cent stamp when he does not want to release the figures showing that a 60-cent stamp would be needed?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before answering that, I want to say that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin), just pointed out that for over 30 years she walked to the post office to pick up her mail and she does not consider herself a second-class citizen as a result of doing that. People who have had that personal experience have to dismiss the accusations of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).
The Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) may be referring to certain figures that were in an editorial in The Toronto Star which supposedly had a different set of figures. That is nonsense. The figures I have quoted to him are in fact from a study the Post Office gave me.
The Hon. Member asks a valid question. Should those figures be made available? Yes, they should, and I will see if I can get them in form to do so.
Very soon, in the not too distant future, the Post Office will be called before the Standing Committee on Government Operations in defence of the Estimates and its corporate plan. That would provide a splendid opportunity for interested Members to go over in detail with senior management of the Canada Post Corporation all of these items. They are there and I have seen them. I have seen the slides and I am sure senior management will bring the slides to the committee so that the Hon. Member can have these numbers verified.
The Hon. Member asks a legitimate question and he will be provided with those numbers. However, I would ask him something in return. If he gets those numbers and they verify what I have indicated, which is what has been indicated to me by Canada Post Corporation, will he commit on behalf of his Party to state, if the Liberals are still in favour of it, that they are in favour of putting in door-to-door mail delivery everywhere where group boxes are now used and they are prepared to have the price of stamps rise in order to pay for that? He shakes his head in the negative. There is a man who says that he wants honesty and openness. Does he want openness? Not at all, Mr. Speaker.
We will give him the figures. Will he commit to have the integrity to give them to the people of Canada as he goes around making promises? Will he tell them how much those promises will cost and how they will be paid for? He is still shaking his head in the negative. At least he is proving that he is a genuine Liberal. He is in the right Party. Never tell the people the truth or they may not elect you, that is what Liberals think.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very simple question for the Minister and it involves the truth. I wonder if he would look into this matter for me and get me some facts and figures.
The kind of society he has been talking about is urban Canada where people go to supermarkets and are able to buy stamps at the same time as they buy groceries. He is not talking about rural Canada or northern Canada. There is another society in which people are hurting, are unemployed and need what comes in the mail. Small businesses and individuals need the mail and they are not getting it.
I just talked to representatives from the post office in Labrador City. Seventy-nine bags of mail destined for Labrador were left in St. John's today. The Minister wants us to commit to an increase in the price of stamps, but the service that is being given by Canada Post, particularly in rural and northern Canada, is absolutely abysmal. Why should we go for an increase in the price of stamps when that kind of service still exists?
Unemployed people need their cheques. Small businessmen are getting things in the mail that they need to survive. Would the Minister find out for me why 79 bags of mail destined for Labrador City were left in St. John's today? This is a specific example of the kind of service the post office is giving. If we can get the facts on that, maybe one of these days, if service improves, we can agree to an increase in the price of stamps.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) makes a valid point. It is interesting that in that connection, there is an innovation that the current management of the Post Office has brought in. It is incredible that this is an innovation because I would think that such a system would have been there for some decades, but it is only within the last three years that Canada Post Corporation has had the ability to answer the question the Hon. Member has raised, why the mail did not go on.
Incredible as it seems to me, up until three years ago, the Post Office operated almost as 11 separate little organizations. There was no central control. There was no ability at headquarters in Ottawa for anyone to know where the mail was at any one time because the mail would come into one of those 11 places, say Calgary, to be sorted. The stuff that was to be delivered in the Calgary area was kept and the rest would be sent to wherever it was to go, to the East or to Vancouver. However, no one at headquarters knew how much mail had
March 24, 1988

been sorted in Calgary, how much had been sent off, where it was at any one time or what was happening.
Now there is a control centre in Ottawa, and I would recommend that Hon. Members take an opportunity to visit it if they have a chance to do so. That control centre is connected to all of the sorting facilities around the country. All of the airline information and the trucking transportation information is there. It is a modern facility and at any one time, the Post Office knows where the mail is.
Why did the mail not get from St. John's to Labrador City?
I do not know. Has there been a storm there? If the airline does not fly, it cannot get the mail there. The Post Office has the same problems everyone else in Canada has when travelling in winter. Sometimes the airlines do not fly and sometimes existing methods of transportation do not work, but at least today someone in Ottawa has the ability to phone St. John's and ask why that mail did not get to Labrador City, give someone hell and hold someone to account. That is a new innovation. If that did not happen already today, I will make that inquiry and whoever is responsible ought to have a good explanation as well as a plan to make sure that it does not happen in the future.
Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question?

speechtext:

I would like to bring to the attention of the Hon. Member that I heard his remarks. I gave the Hon. Member 23 or 24 minutes plus 12 or 14 minutes for questions and comments and I thought that because it was the Minister who spoke, Hon. Members would want to ask more questions of him. That is why I extended his time for a few extra minutes.

Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago, I asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) a very simple question. I asked him to explain to the people who live in the cities and suburbs of Canada why some of them get door-to-door delivery and others have to depend on supermailboxes. The Minister, of course, talked all around the subject. He brought in the question of the kind of service there is in rural and northern areas, a separate question all together.
The fact is that city people resent the fact that they do not get the same service in the suburbs as they got when they lived in the inner city. The Minister had all kinds of explanations for these differences including the fact that there are no sidewalks in areas where there are new housing developments. A resident of Calgary must have been watching this debate because she called my office to point out that the suburban sidewalks are not built not because they are not wanted but because the municipalities cannot afford them. She thinks, and I am quoting from the message we got, that the Minister is quite ignorant on this subject and she is very angry with him.

I want to spend a few minutes on what has happened to the price of prescription drugs in the last half of 1987. The Minister spent part of his time berating those who claim that prices have gone up in the last year much more than the increase in the cost of living would have permitted. Supposedly Bill C-22 would have prevented that. He said those who were making that charge were either lying or were ignorant of the real facts. Here are the real facts as given to the people of Canada by responsible government agencies.
The Government of Ontario found that the price of drugs in its drug plan, and we are not talking about a few drugs but more than 1,000, rose faster than the Consumer Price Index for the six months before the 1987 year end. Some prices went up by 100 per cent and one went up by 250 per cent. Was there anything that could be done about this? Of course. Although the Drug Prices Review Board was set up only in December of 1987, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) said this morning that the board has the authority and the ability to go back five years in determining whether unfair prices have been charged. Why doesn't it do just that?
I have another illustration of what has happened. The Manitoba Government looked at the prices of generic drugs in that province for the last half of 1987 and found that they had actually gone down by 1 per cent. If they went down for generic drugs, why should they have gone up as they did by so much for so many of the brand-name drugs? Why does the Government not try and explain this disparity in more correct ways rather than heaping scorn on those providing the information? It is an old device for Governments to shoot the messenger because he brings bad news rather than deal with reality.
Why is the Government not encouraging the Drug Prices Review Board instead of heaping scorn on the Opposition? It is not just opposition Members of Parliament, it is all consumer groups, seniors, labour organizations and others who warned what would happen if Bill C-22 passed. If necessary, why is the Government not bringing in amendments to give the board the power to roll back prices when they increase by more than the inflation rate? Instead, the Government pretends that nothing is happening, the board is not working, and the Opposition is responsible for the delay. That is not going to fool anyone. The results will be seen in the next election, and I do not expect to see the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs back in this House as a Member of Parliament after the next election.
I now want to deal with the problem hundreds of thousands of people have in their dealings with banks. Bank profits are huge. In 1987 the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce had a profit of S387 million. For Scotia Bank it was $381 million. For the Bank of Montreal, $413 million. For the Toronto-Dominion Bank, $528 million. For the Royal Bank, $541 million. What taxes did they pay? Based on past experience, very little. In many cases no real taxes were paid because the banks have been able to take advantage of our tax system

fact, it is not saving money at all. The banks are increasing their charges continually.
The banks are doing this in part to recoup the losses on money which they lent to Third World countries including Mexico and Brazil, at very attractive rates. They were getting upwards of 20 per cent interest some years ago. They were very happy to make those loans and earn that revenue through the high interest rates charged, particularly since in those years with a Liberal Government the tax system permitted and encouraged them to pay virtually no taxes at all. The banks deny this, but allow me to quote from the business publication Financial Post. In the December 21, 1987, issue an article by Philip Mathias entitled "Nickel-and-diming" says:
Just why fees are rising is a bone of contention. Critics say banks are squeezing consumers in an attempt to recoup some of the money they expect to lose on their colossal loans to Third World countries and Dome Petroleum Ltd.
To digress, Mr. Speaker, there is something very strange in our tax system when Dome Petroleum, which has lost hundreds of millions of dollars and has received huge loans and grants from the federal Government is able, when being sold, to pay its president several million dollars severance pay. Many of Dome's workers would be happy to receive that kind of sympathetic treatment from Dome Petroleum and the Government of Canada, but they are not getting it.
Mr. Mathias goes on to say:
Bankers hotly deny this assertion. Instead, they talk about a "user-pay" philosophy, which unbundles individual bank services and makes the customer who calls for a service pay for it.
Both explanations may be correct.
Service charges started rising rapidly in the early 1980s, a timing that fits neatly with the Third World loans and big corporate lending theory. (Bankers, however, say this is only a coincidence.)
Also, in 1982, it dawned on four big Canadian banks that $3 billion lent to Dome Petroleum was not going to be recovered easily.
They should have known that long before. It continues:
The recession of 1981-82 induced corporations to pay down bank loans rather than borrow. Competition among the banks to lend increased sharply.
At the same time, high interest rates made the cost of loans prohibitive. The banks found it difficult to maintain the traditional 3 -point spread between interest paid to lenders and that charged to borrowers. The top lending-out rate came down.
Spreads have still not recovered fully.
The banks have tried to retaliate.
They did not do this by going after the large and profitable corporations. They did it by going after the ordinary little Canadian who really cannot afford these charges and does not have the knowledge, expertise or time to shop around for cheaper financial services. That is the only advice the present Conservative Government will give ordinary Canadians, but it is always ready to defend corporations and individuals in the highest income bracket.
The banks argue that they are providing better service now to their customers. The automation of many of their services
Supply
should have kept the cost down, but the productivity savings in terms of lower labour cost and overhead are not being passed on to the consumer.
Many credit unions have no service charges at all in return for minimum deposits which also earn interest. Are the chartered banks less efficient than some of the smaller financial institutions? Obviously not. But the credit union represents ordinary people and cares about them. The banks have a captive clientele. They are not interested in looking after ordinary Canadians but in looking after the accounts of large corporations and wealthy individuals.
The advice of this Conservative Government is to shop around and let the buyer beware. Canadians are being criticized for not doing what they should, but most of them are unable to take the Government's advice because they do not have the information needed.
Today, the Minister of State for Finance said that he wants to hear from the Finance Committee. He is aware of the obligation of the banks under the Bank Act. Therefore, why does he have to wait for the recommendation of that committee? The Minister of State for Finance or the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should tell the banks what they are required to do under the provisions of the Bank Act.
The Minister is doing nothing about it because he is not interested in the consumer. The Government is not interested in the small business community, the Consumers' Association or in poverty groups such as the National Anti-Poverty Association, all of whom agree that until the banking committee makes its report there should be an immediate freeze on bank charges. The Government will not do it because its priority is to protect those in whom it is interested, which includes the banks. That is not surprising when one considers the kinds of donations made to the Conservative Party by the major banks.
This motion, and the way the Government has failed to deal with the banks, certainly tells Canadians where the Government stands in terms of trying to protect the interest of ordinary Canadians.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I commend my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton- East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) for bringing this motion to the House today. It is appropriate to review the Tory tax record at this time and consider how the Conservative philosophy and policy has impacted upon M. et Mme tout le monde, as they say in Quebec.
The Tory philosophy seems to be: "Reach out and tax someone". Since they came to office, the Tories have hit Canadians with dozens of new taxes. I am reminded of something that Adam Smith said, which I believe reflects the

March 24, 1988
Supply
Tory point of view about who should shoulder the tax burden in this country. Adam Smith said: "There is no art which one government sooner learns from another than that of draining money from the people". I would suggest that phrase "draining money from the people" has a Conservative epitaph.
Rather than giving itself credit, the Government should be thankful that it came into office at a time when increased growth and an improved economy was taking place throughout the world. Despite being the benefactors of this improved situation, the Government has reached into the pockets of individual Canadian taxpayers to make the biggest tax grab in our history.
The Government's record of taxation reveals that it is showing an increased insensitivity toward lower and middle income families in Canada. Let us consider the tax increases the Government has seen fit to impose on Canadians. In 198485, there were personal income taxes in the amount of $29.3 billion, corporate taxes in the amount of $9.4 billion, and sales and excise taxes of $13.7 billion. In 1988-89, personal income tax will amount to $45.4 billion, $12 billion for corporate income tax, and $24.3 billion in sales and excise taxes.
By the end of the 1989 fiscal year there will be $16.1 billion in personal income tax, an increase of 55 per cent. Corporate tax will amount to $2.6 billion, which is an increase of 28 per cent. Sales and excise taxes will be $10.6 billion, for a 77 per cent increase. When we consider that the sales and excise taxes apply to everyone, whether one is earning $200,000 or $10,000, I suggest that this fact alone indicates the insensitivity and unfairness of the Government.
Furthermore, when we consider the particular areas in which taxation has been levelled, we can see the gross insensitivity of the Government. The fact that there is a 55 per cent increase in personal income tax and only a 28 per cent increase in corporate income tax shows that there is a sense of affinity for the corporate sector. It simply proves the Government has not been fair. Although the Government campaigned on a promise not to raise taxes, it has seen fit to hit Canadians with more than $22 billion in new taxes, to which can be added another $7 billion in future taxes.
The Government has claimed that the lower deficit is due to its ingenious management of the economy. I suggest that the Government's fiscal management has been incredibly poor because there has been an increase in the over-all per capita deficit. The per capita deficit has risen to $300 billion, from $7,000 per capita in 1983 to $12,000, a 60 per cent increase. During a time of high prosperity, the Government's poor management and poor judgment has resulted in that increase in per capita deficit.
These tax increases began with three consecutive sales tax increases, beginning in October, 1984.
The Conservatives hit Canadians with their first tax bite from 9 per cent to 10 per cent, which would subsequently go up to 12 per cent in hidden sales taxes. If one adds it all up, it comes to $3 billion, just in those hidden sales taxes. What that meant was that when men and women went to shop for new clothes, shoes for their children to go to school, food for their homes, the general everyday living, the cost was higher. The Government, through hidden taxes, had increased those costs by $3 billion.
I sometimes think that White Christmas was never on the Government's mind. It imposed a tax on candy, soft drinks, snacks. The cost to Canadians was $460 million, and one can add to that the $60 million which was added in taxes on paint and wallpaper. What kind of incentive is that for homeowners to improve their property? It was certainly a disincentive. I suggest that although it may have been hard on the redecorating bills at 24 Sussex Drive, it was equally hard, if not much harder, on the pocketbooks of ordinary Canadians.
I think we should be reminded that in this latest Budget the Tories put an incredible additional tax on gasoline. The first tax was worth $900 million. There was another tax of $450 million. There was one more additional tax of $450 million. If that was not enough, we have now had an increase of 23 cents per litre, which is close to one dollar per gallon for gas since September of 1985. This new tax of one cent a litre will come in April 1 and the Government will recover $450 million from that.
I would suggest we consider that $2.1 billion the Government is pulling in on that gas tax. I think there is a gas pipe that leads directly to the revenue treasury producing money for the Government to spend in all kinds of ridiculous areas. I wish they would increase spending in areas that are important to Canada.
I think we should consider the impact on workers who drive to work. The impact on their daily lives has been very significant. I think it is very unfair.
There was $700 million taken in by the Government from the increased tax on alcohol and tobacco. It is nice the Government is looking after our health and well-being, but some of us like those little luxuries and I think it is a little unfair. Then, of course, there is the marvellous tax on talking which quietly came into effect on January 1 of this year. Long distance telephone charges went up. They are now subject to a 10 per cent tax and the cost to Canadians is $945 million. Because of the strange way the lines are drawn for local and long-distance calls, many families will have to pay that additional tax every time they call their doctors or their dentists and-

It does not apply to residential phones and you know that.

That is very interesting. I am glad the Minister has clarified that. We will just say that the tax is only costing $945 million for long-distance business calls. I am glad to hear that.
We must not forget the income tax changes. Canadians have not been able to forget the direct cash withdrawal from the pockets of consumers. I suggest that in those income tax changes, we have had the deindexing of the whole tax system. That small bill comes to $635 million on which we will add another 3 per cent next year and another 3 per cent the year after that. It goes on ad nauseam. The Government killed the Registered Homeownership Savings Plan, which certainly was a help to young people buying their first homes. That cost families $105 million.
We then had the elimination of the tax abatement clause. It added some very nice cash into the pockets of the Government. That is where the Government collects money and then holds it and sends it back to you without bothering to pay you interest. That will cost $650 million. That is not bad. There is also the temporary 5 per cent and 10 per cent surtax on high-income earners. However, that was only in effect from July 1, 1985 to December 31, 1986. There must have been a big lobby that told the Government to stop that. That only cost us $500 million.
There were the changes in tax treatment of dividend income which brought in another $300 million. There was a change in spousal exemptions. Those are the married benefits. It is a small amount of money, only $20 million. That is what the Government thinks about the role of the spouse within the family.
As I mentioned, all these taxes I have talked about, the sprinkling of these dozens of tax grabs by the Government, from individuals, families, senior citizens, total $22 billion. We should compare that with the fact that many corporations in this country still do not pay taxes and there is $1 billion of outstanding taxes to be collected from these corporations, on which Revenue Canada has not followed up. Why is it not doing its job? I think that $1 billion might offset some of the other things which I find rather regressive.
It does not take long to figure out who are the friends of this Government. If it is true that Canadians often vote with their pocketbooks, they surely will remember this Government on the way to the polls. So far I have spoken now just with respect to the hidden taxes and the overt taxes. What about the new tax treat the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is planning for us? We do not have the amount it is going to cost the taxpayers with respect to the new sales tax the Government intends to introduce after the next election. I would suggest that one part of that is a horrible Tory proposal. Fortunately, the Minister backed off on the tax on food but it took a whole brouhaha. It
Supply
took weeks of questioning in this House before the Minister rose and clarified that he will not tax perishable foods in the new sales tax. He will tax wax-paper, Saran Wrap and soap, all the things one uses to run one's home, but not one's food, according to the Minister of Finance.
There was an unfortunate leak that occurred when the Committee on Finance came back from New Zealand. There seemed to be some indication that it found that a tax on food was a good idea. It then withdrew that proposal. I would hope that never again will those words "tax on food" come forward and that that idea is rejected out of hand.
For the Government to put its hand in the pockets of working Canadians to the extent of $22 billion is a pretty sad situation. The Government says it is staying the course. Staying the course will certainly not help the 3.7 million Canadians who are living below the poverty line, nor those women whose revenue has fallen even further below the wages of men, nor the homeless, those people who are living on the streets, and those people who are going to the food banks.
I would suggest that staying the course and offering no plan of action is an affront to the many Canadians who have a right to look to the Government for leadership. I am truly saddened at the inadequate response to the despair that is being experienced in this country. I strongly recommend that the Government take a good look at where the real problems are and start addressing some of those serious concerns in this country.
If the Government is going to drain $22 billion in the largest tax grab in the history of this country, it should use some of that to help in job retraining, youth access, or for elderly people and their concerns, their access to the market, and their dislocation. Over three and a half years there have been many places where the Government could have done something constructive instead of a do nothing, stay the course Budget with no new initiatives or measures to assist the needy.
I think that the concept of free trade will cost Canadians very dearly. Has the Government forgotten that the consumer of this country is also the voter? I was going to address the question of bank charges and the incredibly huge charges that are hidden. 1 hope that the Government will move in that regard in order that people can have choices. If the Government would insist that there be open and full disclosure, we might well have signs up in the banks. Then we could do some comparative shopping and the bank charges and bank rates might be more open to general society.
If what is happening under free trade is looked at very carefully, the Canadian consumer will pay for this free trade initiative. For only the removal of the tariffs it will cost $1.5 billion this year, $1 billion next year, and $2 billion the year after. That wipes out the half of one per cent growth per year that we are supposed to have. How will we pay for that? I think that we will have to find someone to pay for additional

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
The Elon. Member for Westmount speaks so sincerely that Canadians may be tempted to believe her. I am amazed that she would have the gall to misrepresent so many basic things. I was immediately taken aback when she had the nerve to tell people that we have driven up the price of gasoline in this country since taking office.
When I was elected in 1984, the price of gasoline in my Province of Prince Edward Island was in the vicinity of 56 cents a litre. Today that same litre costs 48 cents. A quick conversion of approximately 8 cents a litre works out to approximately 36 cents a gallon. If one fills the tank and it is only 10 gallons, that is a saving of $3.60. If it is 15 gallons, that is a saving of $5.40 every time one goes to the pumps. That is a big saving.
Through the National Energy Program, the Liberal Government not only drove the price of gasoline up for every Canadian, but it ruined the whole oil industry in this country and set us back by years. Thank goodness our Government has done some things that have begun to turn this around.
The other thing that the Government has done in relation to gasoline is continue to rebate all the excise tax and sales tax to Canadian farmers. Many of the same things have been done for fishermen and for primary producers.
In the Province of Prince Edward Island the price of fuel not only affects the cost of gasoline, but it affects the cost of electric power. We buy power under a fuel clause in an agreement with the Province of New Brunswick. Every time that gasoline or fuel increased in the country, our price of electricity increased. Turning on the switch became a very expensive proposition.
In the same manner as we dropped the price of gasoline by getting rid of the NEP and returning to some rational order, we have also dropped the price of electricity to Prince Edward Island consumers. Those are two major areas where the Government has done much for the average person.
The Hon. Member talked about interest rates. I recall when interest rates were 22 and 23 per cent, bankrupting farmers, fishermen, and small business. The country was in ruins. Unemployment was rampant all over the place. We were wondering where it was going to end. Of course, it ended with the defeat of the former Liberal Government, and we started to restore some order.
My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) moved quickly to bring down interest rates to farmers. Under the Farm Credit Corporation, interest rates dropped by a matter of policy by 4 per cent from 16.75 per cent to 12.75 per cent. One can imagine the thousands of dollars that one move alone would save a medium to large size farmer in this country. It is quite astronomical. Because of the Government's policy, interest rates have come down right across the board. That means that homeowners and small businessmen are saving thousands and thousands of dollars that they otherwise would have had to pay out on mortgage payments, and so on.
I did not plan to rise, but I just could not take it any longer. I am sure that Canadians did not believe the Hon. Member when she was speaking. I am sure they would not want to return to the Liberal Government of a few years ago where the country was on a collision course because of high interest rates, high unemployment, bankruptcies, and continued economic problems and woes from one end of the country to the other.

First, I wish to advise my hon. friend that I am not the Member for Westmount. I am the Member for Mount Royal and quite proud of that. I am pleasantly surprised to think that I have gall; perhaps guile but not gall. I do not think that I was showing too much nerve. I thought I was telling the direct truth. I would like to ask the Hon. Member to please read his Minister's tax Budgets. In case he cannot read, the Minister imposed a 2 cent per litre tax on September 3, 1985, and a 1 cent per litre tax on January 1, 1987, the first increase bringing in $900 million, the second increase bringing in $450 million, and 1 cent per litre on February 19, 1987, bringing in another $450 million. In case the Hon. Member does not look or does not know because this is a sneaky, hidden, indirect tax, there will be an additional 1 cent per litre increase as of April 1 of this year. I suggest the Hon. Member watch the pump. When the Hon. Member adds up $450 million, $450 million, and $900 million, the total is $2.1 billion added on to the tax bill of someone who knows what he is talking about and goes to the pump. First, I wish to advise the Hon. Member about that.
Second, the Hon. Member is very excited about how well he is doing in the supplying of energy either through oil or through hydroelectricity. That is great. The only thing the Hon. Member has forgotten is that he has given away our sovereign right to make some decisions around energy in this free trade deal. The Hon. Member ought to return and look at that too.
When the Hon. Member is talking about the farmers, I think he forgot about the marketing boards and the fact that farmers will have one heck of a job under free trade when they have to reconcile the marketing board, and the Canadian environment of snow six, seven months of the year, against the Americans south of the border with nice, warm twelve months a year grow-my-own products.

I was moved and generally enthralled by the level of debate by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs.
March 24, 1988

Finestone) and the very thoughtful remarks of my colleague from Prince Edward Island. I felt that I must be moved to participate in some small part of this.
I wanted to ask the Hon. Member a little more about the question of taxation in terms of gas and generally the question of energy policy. The Hon. Member will know that in terms of deficit reduction-and this involves the obscenely high deficit that the Government inherited and the high national debt-it is being ratcheted down by using, roughly, a 70-30 formula. Some 70 per cent of the deficit reduction is being done by the Government simply taking less in contracting, and 30 per cent is being done by higher taxes.
If the Hon. Member considers the removal of the National Energy Program, the deregulation of natural gas and crude oil, the concurrent drop in world prices, even with the taxes which she as a Montreal Member of Parliament so greatly laments, and the free trade agreement that will indeed make Canada stronger and more secure in its energy supplies, how can this member of the Liberal Party stand in her place as an architect of the National Energy Program and purport to speak to Canadians or on behalf of Canadians in the oil and gas issue?
In terms of what is happening now to energy policy in Canada, will she concede that Canada's energy supplies in future are indeed more promising and the future considerably brighter under this Government and what we have done for western Canada?
