What do you say to Canadians who can only watch the mailman go by their door? What do you tell them? Are they not entitled to the same services as their neighbours? Finally, what do you say to the many consumers who were used to paying a minimal charge for Government services and who in many cases are now faced with increases of 200, 300 and 400 per cent? What do you tell them? The fact is that you have overloaded the consumer with taxes just so you would be in a position to reduce the taxes of others that can afford to pay, and I mean major companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to smile at the comments of the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif), who begins by saying: We spent more than we could afford, and should have in order to help consumers because there was an economic crisis.
I recognize that there was a recession between 1980 and 1983. The figures I quoted related to the period when his Leader was Minister of Finance between 1971 and 1975. This is when, according to the C.D. Howe Institute, and I shall now repeat it, as the Hon. Member may not have understood, most of Mr. Turner's budgets disturbed the relative balance of economic positions by favouring very high and/or lower middle income families rather than the poor.
When Mr. Turner was Minister of Finance, the poor and the needy were not the ones to be protected against inflation. Monetary benefits went mostly to the wealthiest 8 per cent of Canadian families. These comments were not made by Conservative supporters, but by the C.D. Howe Institute.
The Hon. Member says that his Government spent more during the recession to help consumers, but I challenge him to say where, in the Trois-Rivieres riding, it made any investments which really helped to create permanent jobs or did anything really useful for the riding. All its initiatives amounted to flagrant patronage and patching. This is all it did. It said it was creating jobs by doing some construction work. As everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, jobs in construction are not permanent jobs. It is only a band-aid solution. This is what the previous Government did when it talked about job creation.

March 24, 1988

As for us, Mr. Speaker, in co-operation with the private sector, we have created 1.3 million jobs since September 1984. Moreover, 80 per cent have been permanent jobs and a lot of them have gone to women and young people, which had never been the case under the previous Liberal Government.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member raised the question of hydroelectricity. It is a subject that is very dear to my heart.
There is about 10,000 megawatts of electricity in Labrador flowing to the sea every day, untapped, unrestrained. This is happening in a province which will run out of electricity in 1992. In a province which will have no more of electricity in 1992, 10,000 megawatts of electricity flows to the sea every day. That is not the problem of the Hon. Member, I know, but I want to try to put that in context if I can.
The Hon. Member talked about the value of the free trade agreement. I hope he will listen to this because I have some arguments to make and I hope he will want to reply to them later on.
Not only is it impossible to develop that hydroelectricity now without the help of the Province of Quebec, a province which takes about $800 to every $8 that goes to the Province of Newfoundland for the Upper Churchill contract, but it will be doubly difficult to do so in the future under the free trade agreement. Every province that wants to export electricity must pass a test. First, they must pass a price test and second, they must ask other provinces if they want their power. They cannot sell electricity to the U.S. unless they ask the other provinces if they want the power.
In future, the provinces will not have to do that, not simply because of free trade but because of the deregulation policy of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse). In a moment, I would like to quote the Minister of Energy because his words are apropos to what the free trade deal does.
The free trade deal creates a level playing field. It provides that we are no different from the Americans. I see that the Hon. Member is leaving. Perhaps I will repeat my point when he returns.
In future, we will be no different from the Americans. We will not be able to have a made-in-Canada price. The National Energy Program which has been very much maligned today allowed Canada to have a Canadian price, but we cannot do so any longer. The free trade deal says that we are a level playing field.
We are talking about consumers here today. It is great to develop James Bay. It will be great for the construction industry. It will provide a lot of construction jobs, and that is good. I applaud Mr. Bourassa for that and I say to my colleagues from Quebec that that is well done, they will create
lots of jobs in the construction stage. However, what will it do to the consumer? There will be no Canadian price for hydroelectricity.
Moreover, apart from free trade, Mr. Masse has said:
To take advantage of these opportunities, federal electricity export policies must change. We need to acknowledge that provincial regulation has become much more sophisticated since 1963, and that there is no need for the federal government to duplicate what the provinces are already doing.
Our general policy framework needs to be more market-oriented. We need to give exporters greater latitude, so that they can concentrate more on business. And we need to streamline the export review process so that it provides incentives for utilities to be more self-regulating.
In other words, the Government is getting out of the way and industry can do what it wants. It does not have to ask the other provinces if they want the electricity and it does not have to offer it to them at a Canadian price. That is the effect of both free trade and the deregulation policies of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The Minister does not have to ask Newfoundland if it wants the power. The Minister does not have to ask Prince Edward Island if it wants the power. The Minister does not have to ask New Brunswick if it wants the power. What will happen to the consumers in those provinces? That is what we are talking about today, consumers and what will happen to the consumers of hydro-electricity under free trade and the deregulation of Mr. Masse.
Not only will the Minister not have to offer power to Prince Edward Island at a decent price, he will not have to offer it to the province at all. That is the effect of the free trade deal coupled with the deregulation policy of Mr. Masse. The provinces that do not have access to power will have less access to it in future, and even if they are offered it out of the goodness of the hearts of those producing it, they will have to pay the American price. That is the effect of free trade and the deregulation policy of Mr. Masse.
As I say, it is great for the construction industry in Quebec and it is great for people who want jobs-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I bring to the attention of the Hon. Member that he is mentioning the Hon. Minister's name when he should be saying the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse). He has done it three times and that is the only reason I bring it to his attention.

We have to say things over and over so that the people opposite will understand, but I do appreciate your point, Mr. Speaker, and I apologize for that.
Joe Smallwood, and I can mention his name because he never was in this Chamber, always used to say that you have to tell people what you are going to say, then you have to say it and then you have to tell people what you already said in order to get the message across. I want to make sure that I get the message across that free trade plus the deregulation policy of the Minister of Energy will have a negative impact on the consumer in provinces which do not produce hydroelectricity.
March 24, 1988

It may even have a negative impact on the consumers of hydroelectricity in Quebec itself. I cannot speak for that province, but I can speak for my own.
That is the response I would make to the Hon. Member about hydroelectricity. Of course, there are many other points to be made too, and they have been made adequately today. My colleague from Mount Royal and others have sketched out the taxes that have been increased over the years, particularly the sales tax which of course is a regressive tax because it impacts negatively on those people who have less and it does not, however, impact a great deal on those who have more.
There have been tax increases and they have been regressive. They have not been a help to the consumers of Canada. The Government, of course, says that it can do this because the economy is good and because it has created a lot of jobs. Therefore, there is more income and businesses are investing more and creating more jobs. Where is that happening? In central Canada. Sure, there are more jobs in Toronto, but how many have been created in the Atlantic provinces?
If the argument is that you can increase taxes because the economy is good and business has invested and created more jobs, then the effect of increased taxes is doubly damaging to people in areas where the jobs have not been created, where there is still high unemployment, and where incomes are still low. In the Province of Newfoundland we still have the lowest per capita income and the highest unemployment rate in the country. What is the effect of tax increases on people in that area?
What about gasoline taxes? How many things come in to that province by truck? Quite a lot, and as gasoline goes up, prices go up. Berthage fees for fishermen have been increased. At the same time there have been cuts in government programs across the board in order to cut the deficit. That, too, has a cumulative effect on consumers, particularly in have-not provinces which are dependent upon government programs.
Then on top of that is the issue I raised with the Minister responsible for the Post Office concerning the state of our mail service. He talked about the fact that people wanted to go to supermarkets and collect their stamps at the same time they collected their groceries. That is fine for urban Canada but it does not work that way in rural Canada or northern Canada. He was asking for an increase in the price of stamps so he could improve mail service. I pointed out that the level of service we get in the North is deplorable. I talked to the Post Office today in Labrador City. Seventy-nine bags of mail destined for Labrador City were left in the airport in St. John's. Labrador City is served only by air. There are no ships that go there and no roads. People there depend on the mail service. The unemployed, pensioners and those on fixed incomes depend on it for cheques. They are consumers. Yet the Post Office wants to increase the cost of stamps while still
Supply
providing that deplorable service. Before they get that increase they better clean up their act and start giving decent service.
Then there is the impact of other government policies. We have not talked about young people and the effect on them of government policies. They are consumers, or they want to be. The fact is that money for post-secondary education has been decreased. The fact is there is a 30 per cent drop in funding to community colleges and CEGEPs as a result of the change in the Canadian Jobs Strategy. The fact is that the amount of money for summer jobs for young people has been frozen for the past three years. There is a direct correlation between the amount of education you have and the amount of money you earn. If young people want to be consumers, where is the incentive to get an education and try and start their own business? It is not there. This is a factor we have to consider.
I want to point out that even fisheries policy has an effect on consumers. I know of a fish plant in my riding right now that will have to lay off workers this summer, 56 people. Not a large number, perhaps, but in a community of 500 or 600, almost the total workforce in that plant will be laid off this summer. Why? It is a fisherman's co-op, the Labrador Lishermen's Union Shrimp Company, and the Government has said it cannot have a supply of offshore fish. The Government is prepared to bargain away that fish to Trance, but it has told the fishermen on that coast that they cannot have access to fish. That situation has a direct connection to consumers because once you start doing away with jobs, you start doing away with the wherewithal to make purchases. That aspect of government policy has its effect, too.
It seems to me that over the past four years, while businesses in certain parts of the country may have expanded and employment may have been created, the over-all effect on consumers has not been positive from the point of view of the broad range of government policy. That is the situation and I think that when this Government goes to its accountability session, as it must very soon, possibly this fall, the people of Canada will judge. If the polls are any indication, then the consumers of Canada will judge harshly indeed.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Grand Tails-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) spoke about saying something three times to get the crowd on this side of the House to understand what he is saying. I want to say that the crowd on this side of the House believe in doing instead of talking.
He spoke about harbours. When this Conservative Government came into office in 1984, the harbours around Canada were generally in poor condition. Many of them were in an advanced state of disrepair so as to render them unsafe. At that time it was estimated that approximately 112 harbours were indeed unsafe for vessels seeking safe haven. Many of them were barricaded. It does not sound like the previous Government had looked after the fishermen or recreational users in a very good way as far as the harbours were concerned.

March 24, 1988
Supply
At that time, if corrective measures had not been taken, in another five years an additional 150 harbours would have to have been closed. These statistics were and are alarming since the livelihood of fishermen is at stake. Most of the small craft harbours operated through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans are located in outlying areas where fishing represents the primary source of income. That situation could not be condoned by this Government and I am glad to say that the Minister announced this past year that $150 million would be spent over the next three years on revitalization and maintenance programs in every province of Canada.
In the motion before us reference is made to user fees. I believe that this has been put in there intentionally to try and scare fishermen into believing that because a plan is being put in place to give fishermen more say in the development of their harbours through local harbour authorities, for some reason or other they are going to have to pay more for the services. I do not believe that that is true. The fishermen to whom I have spoken in the harbours in my constituency welcome the chance to be part of harbour authorities and to be part of the planning for the development which will take place in their harbours. They welcome the chance to set fees for themselves because they know that that money will go back to them for them to administer and use to their own advantage.
It is interesting to note that some of these harbours will be leased to harbour authorities which will help the federal Government set out directions for the setting of priorities for improvement and development of their harbours. As I have already said, they will undertake the day-to-day management. They will be able to install electricity on wharfs where they want it to use to their own advantage. The same is true with water on the wharfs.
Some people in my constituency have already approached me about setting up marinas in harbours which are presently used mainly by fishermen. They know that there are more tourists coming in from different parts of Canada and from the United States and they want to be able to provide harbour facilities to these people in order to generate more revenue to use for their own advantage.
Giving local fishermen, members of town councils or development associations and others the opportunity to serve on the harbour authorities will establish grass roots user management. They will be able to match programs more precisely to local needs and set their own priorities.
As I said, I believe that this motion is only a scare tactic of the Opposition such as those used on many occasions to try to put fear into the people. However, I know that the people in my riding are not fooled by those tactics. They are very grateful for the revitalization program.
The Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador talks about cut-backs. That is certainly not the indication of people in places like Grate's Cove who have been waiting for
harbour facilities for 35 years, ever since Confederation. It is only now, with a Conservative Government, that they are getting those long needed facilities.
